units.title: Your Starter Pack
units.desc: The words you already know, corrected and in proper Jyutping

words.note: Many Hongkongers drop the ng-: 'o5'. Both are fine.

ex.en: I want to go running.

words.note: Often said 'lei5' (n→l). There's no special polite 'you' in everyday Cantonese.

ex.en: Are you going?

words.note: One word for he, she and it — no gender in speech.

ex.en: He's my little brother.

words.note: Links two nouns: 我係家明 (ngo5 hai6 gaa1 ming4) = I'm Ka-ming. 係啊 (hai6 aa3)！ = Yes, that's right.

ex.en: I'm Ka-ming.

words.note: Put it before a verb or adjective: 唔食 (m4 sik6) = don't eat. Just hum 'm' with closed lips, low and falling.

ex.en: I don't eat beef.

words.note: 喺 (hai2) 'at' rises; 係 (hai6) 'to be' is low and flat. Don't mix them up!

ex.en: I'm at home now.

words.note: 好 (hou2) + adjective = very: 好甜 (hou2 tim4) = very sweet. 好啊 (hou2 aa3)！ = OK, sure!

ex.en: So sweet!

words.note: No word for 'to': 去香港 (heoi3 hoeng1 gong2) = go to Hong Kong.

ex.en: Where are you going?

words.note: Compare 識 (sik1) 'to know': same syllable, high tone.

ex.en: Do you eat pork?

words.note: 睇電視 (tai2 din6 si6) = watch TV. The Mandarin word 看 (hon3) is not used in speech.

ex.en: I like watching TV.

words.note: To ask: 有冇 (jau5 mou5)…？ = Do you have…? / Is there…?

ex.en: Do you have a bike?

words.fr: ne pas avoir ; il n'y a pas
words.note: The negative of 有 (jau5). Never say 唔有 (m4 jau5).

ex.en: I don't have a little sister.

words.note: Verb + 緊 (gan2) = doing it now: 食緊 (sik6 gan2) = eating. You already know 落緊雨 (lok6 gan2 jyu5) 'it's raining'!

ex.en: She's watching TV.
Why?
How do I get there?

words.note: Short, everyday form of 乜嘢 (mat1 je5).

ex.en: What do you want?
What do you want to do?
Where is your home?
Which one do you like?

words.note: Polite version of 邊個 (bin1 go3), e.g. on the phone.

ex.en: Who's speaking, please?
My big brother likes running.
Where's my little brother?
My little sister is sleeping.

words.note: Means 'home'. A house as a building is 屋 (uk1).

ex.en: My big brother is at home.
I want to sleep.
I like fish.

words.note: Don't mix with 咗 (zo2), which marks a finished action.

ex.en: What are you doing?

sentences.en: Where is your big brother?
She is my little sister.
Why aren't you going?
What do you like to eat?
I really like my home.
Where is your home?

grammar.title: Questions go where the answer goes
grammar.explain: Cantonese doesn't move question words to the front. Say the statement and drop 邊度 (bin1 dou6) / 咩 (me1) / 邊個 (bin1 go3) into the slot of the answer.

examples.en: I want to go to your home.
What do you want to eat?

grammar.title: Saying no: 唔 (m4) and 冇 (mou5)
grammar.explain: 唔 (m4) goes in front of a verb or adjective: 唔食 (m4 sik6), 唔難 (m4 naan4). For 有 (jau5) 'have', the negative is 冇 (mou5).

examples.en: I don't have a little brother.

units.title: Tone Primer
units.desc: Hear the six tones, read Jyutping, and hear tones in words you already know

words.note: Tone 1 · high and flat, like holding a high note.
Tone 2 · starts mid and rises high, like a surprised 'eh?'.
Tone 3 · mid and flat, your normal speaking pitch.
Tone 4 · low and falling, the bottom of your voice.
Tone 5 · starts low and rises only to mid — a smaller rise than tone 2.
Tone 6 · low and flat, just under tone 3.
Tone 1 + tone 1: both syllables high and level. Keep the pitch up for the whole word.
Tone 2 rises from mid to high, then tone 1 stays high and level.
Tone 2: rises from mid to high, like a surprised "eh?". oe ≈ French "eu".
Tone 1 then tone 3: high, then your normal mid pitch.
Tone 4 then tone 1: start at the bottom of your voice, jump to the top.
Tone 6 + tone 6: low and level, just under your normal pitch.
Tone 4: low and falling. Compare 點 (dim2), which rises.
Tone 4, long aa. Compare 行 (haang4) "to walk": same tone, but it ends in -ng.

grammar.title: Six tones, one chart
grammar.explain: Pitch is part of the word. Imagine your voice range as 5 steps: tone 1 sits at the top (5), tone 3 in the middle (3), tone 6 just below (2), tone 4 drops to the bottom (1). Tone 2 rises from the middle to the top (3→5); tone 5 rises only a little, from low to mid (2→3). Every Jyutping syllable ends with its tone number.

examples.en: poem, history, try, time, market, matter

grammar.title: Reading Jyutping
grammar.explain: j = English y · z ≈ ts without a puff of air (close to 'dz') · c ≈ ts with a puff of air · yu = French u · eo / oe ≈ French eu · aa is long, a is short · final -p, -t, -k are not released: the syllable is just cut short.

units.title: Your Everyday Words
units.desc: More of the words you already know: your day, food and things at home

words.en: week; day of the week (+ number)
words.note: 星期一 (sing1 kei4 jat1) Monday … 星期六 (sing1 kei4 luk6) Saturday, 星期日 (sing1 kei4 jat6) Sunday.

ex.en: I go running on Mondays.

words.note: Keep the h-: ho2 ji5. Dropping h- is not one of the usual casual sound changes, so 'o2 ji5' sounds off.

ex.en: Can I go?
I want beef.

words.note: Also written 俾 (bei2). 'I give' = 我畀 (ngo5 bei2).

ex.en: Pass me a tissue, would you?

words.note: Not the same as 鹹 (haam4, salty): -ng vs -m ending.

ex.en: I really like walking.
I'm going shopping with my big sister.
Pork and beef.

words.note: 同 (tung4) alone = 'with'. 同埋 (tung4 maai4) = 'and / together with'.
Sugar itself is 糖 (tong4).

ex.en: I don't like sweet things.

words.note: Many Hongkongers say 'laan4' (n→l). Both are understood.

ex.en: Cantonese is very difficult!

words.note: 落雨 (lok6 jyu5) = to rain; 緊 (gan2) = -ing. There is no 'I' in it.

ex.en: It's raining — I'm not going.

words.note: Often said 'au4 juk6' without the ng-.
Alone it's usually jyu2; in compounds jyu4 (e.g. 魚蛋 (jyu4 daan2)).

ex.en: My little sister doesn't eat fish.
My little brother doesn't like lamb.

words.note: Your 'chizi' sounds like 廁紙 (ci3 zi2) = toilet paper! A napkin is 紙巾 (zi2 gan1).
Often said 'din6 lou5'. Compare 電爐 (din6 lou4) — only the tone differs!

ex.en: Do you have a computer?

sentences.en: My big brother and big sister are in Hong Kong.
Why are you sleeping now?
I like riding my bike.
It's raining, I don't want to go running.
Can I use the computer?
This fish is very salty.
How do you use this appliance?
My big sister likes sweet things.
Who wants pork?
Why don't you eat pork?
Which day are you going shopping?
He has a computer but no TV.

grammar.title: 想 (soeng2) vs 想要 (soeng2 jiu3)
grammar.explain: 想 (soeng2) + verb = want to do. 想要 (soeng2 jiu3) + thing = want a thing.

grammar.title: 緊 (gan2): happening right now
grammar.explain: Put 緊 (gan2) straight after the verb to say something is going on right now, like English '-ing'.

examples.en: It's raining — where are you going?

dialogue.title: At home on a rainy day

lines.en: What are you doing?
I'm watching TV.
Do you want to go running?
It's raining. I don't want to.
Then let's go shopping!
OK! Where to?

questions.q: What is B doing at first?
Why doesn't B want to go running?
What do they decide to do?

units.title: Hello & Thanks
units.desc: Greet people, say thanks and sorry, and get by when you don't understand

words.note: Fine with strangers. Friends just say the person's name, or 早晨 (zou2 san4) in the morning. The textbook 你好嗎 (nei5 hou2 maa3)？ sounds stiff — see 最近點啊 (zeoi3 gan6 dim2 aa3).

ex.en: Hello, I'm Ka-ming.

words.note: Used until about 11 a.m. There is no common 'good afternoon' — just say 你好 (nei5 hou2).

ex.en: Good morning, Mr Chan!

words.note: Literally 'rest early'. Said when going to bed or leaving late at night — not 'good evening'.

ex.en: Good night! I'm off to bed.

words.note: From English 'bye-bye'; the most common goodbye in Hong Kong. 再見 (zoi3 gin3) is more formal.

ex.en: OK, bye!

words.note: Use it when someone does something for you, to call a waiter, or to get past people. 唔該晒 (m4 goi1 saai3) = thanks a lot. The reply is 唔使唔該 (m4 sai2 m4 goi1) 'no need to thank'.

ex.en: Excuse me, I'd like some pork.

words.note: For gifts, compliments and invitations. 多謝晒 (do1 ze6 saai3) = thanks very much.

ex.en: Thank you!

words.note: A real apology. For small things (interrupting, saying no) use 唔好意思 (m4 hou2 ji3 si1).

ex.en: Sorry! Are you OK?
Sorry, I can't go.
Never mind, I'm fine.
No problem, go ahead and use it!

words.note: Literally 'lately how?'. The everyday 'how are you'.

ex.en: Mr Chan, how have you been?

words.note: 幾 (gei2) before an adjective = 'quite'. 都幾好 (dou1 gei2 hou2) = actually quite good.

ex.en: He's pretty good, thanks.

words.note: At the end of a sentence it makes you sound friendly instead of blunt: 好啊 (hou2 aa3)！ = Sure!

ex.en: What are you eating?

words.note: 你呢 (nei5 ne1)？ = And you? Not the same as 呢 (ni1) 'this' in 呢個 (ni1 go3).

ex.en: I don't eat pork — what about you?

words.note: Makes an invitation or a friendly push: 去啦 (heoi3 laa1)！ = Come on, let's go!

ex.en: OK, let's go!

words.note: Your most useful survival phrase. 明 (ming4) = to understand.

ex.en: Sorry, I don't understand.

words.note: 慢 (maan6) = slow, 啲 (di1) = a bit more. Say it with 唔該 (m4 goi1): 唔該講慢啲 (m4 goi1 gong2 maan6 di1)！

ex.en: Could you speak more slowly, please?

words.note: Literally 'again say one more time'. 唔該再講多次 (m4 goi1 zoi3 gong2 do1 ci3) = Could you say that again, please?

ex.en: Pardon? Please say that again.

words.note: Casual and very common. With strangers, add 唔好意思 (m4 hou2 ji3 si1) first.

ex.en: What? Where are you going?

words.note: X 廣東話點講 (gwong2 dung1 waa2 dim2 gong2)？ = How do you say X in Cantonese? 廣東話 (gwong2 dung1 waa2) = Cantonese.

ex.en: How do you say 'thanks' in Cantonese?

words.note: The polite word in restaurants and malls. At home people say 廁所 (ci3 so2).

ex.en: Excuse me, where's the toilet?

words.note: Literally 'no thing'. 你冇嘢吖嘛 (nei5 mou5 je5 aa1 maa3)？ = You OK? — 冇嘢 (mou5 je5)！ = I'm fine!

ex.en: Nothing — I'm just watching TV.

words.note: Surprise, good or bad. Said with feeling and often drawn out — many people say it waa3.

ex.en: Wow, that's salty!

words.note: Shout it when something good happens. The opposite feeling is 唉 (aai1) 'sigh'.

ex.en: Yay! Let's go shopping!

words.note: 一陣 (jat1 zan6) = a moment, 見 (gin3) = see. For later the same day.

ex.en: OK, see you in a bit!

words.note: 彩 (coi2) means 'luck' here, as in a lucky draw. Said alone, 好彩 (hou2 coi2)！ = Phew, lucky!

ex.en: Luckily, I'm fine.

sentences.en: Good morning, Mr Chan! How have you been?
Pretty good, thanks. And you?
Excuse me, are you Ka-ming?
No, I'm his big brother.
Sorry, I don't eat beef.
Please speak more slowly — I don't understand.
Luckily, he's OK.
Good night, big sister!
Thank you! I really like it!
Is your big sister well?
No problem, I'll go with you.
Bye, see you in a bit!
Wow, your little brother really loves fish!

grammar.title: 唔該 (m4 goi1) or 多謝 (do1 ze6)?
grammar.explain: 唔該 (m4 goi1) thanks someone for doing something for you (a service, a small favour) and also means 'excuse me'. 多謝 (do1 ze6) thanks someone for a gift, a compliment or an invitation.

examples.en: Excuse me, I'd like a napkin.

grammar.title: Yes/no questions: A-唔 (m4)-A
grammar.explain: Repeat the verb with 唔 (m4) in the middle: 係唔係 (hai6 m4 hai6), 食唔食 (sik6 m4 sik6); with two-syllable verbs only the first syllable repeats: 鍾唔鍾意 (zung1 m4 zung1 ji3). There's no single word for 'yes' or 'no' — answer with the verb (係 (hai6)) or its negative (唔係 (m4 hai6)).

grammar.title: 啊 (aa3) makes you sound friendly
grammar.explain: A question or answer without a final particle can sound blunt. Add 啊 (aa3) at the end and it sounds warm and natural.

grammar.title: 呢 (ne1) = and…?
grammar.explain: Put 呢 (ne1) after a person or thing to bounce the question back: 你呢 (nei5 ne1)？ = And you? 你細佬呢 (nei5 sai3 lou2 ne1)？ = And your little brother?

grammar.title: 啦 (laa1) = go ahead / let's
grammar.explain: At the end of a sentence, 啦 (laa1) turns it into a friendly suggestion or invitation.

lines.en: Oops, sorry!
I'm fine, never mind. Oh, Ka-ming, good morning!
Good morning, Mr Chan! How have you been?
Pretty good, thanks. Where are you going?
I'm going running.
But it's raining!
Pardon?
It's RAINING!
No problem! I like running in the rain!
Haha, OK then, bye!
Bye, see you later!

questions.q: How has Mr Chan been?
Where is Ka-ming going?
Why does Mr Chan repeat himself?
What time of day is it?

card.title: Three flat tones
card.explain: Tones 1, 3 and 6 don't move: tone 1 is high, tone 3 is your normal mid pitch, tone 6 sits just under it. Hold the pitch steady from start to finish.

items.note: Tone 1 · high and flat.
Tone 3 · mid and flat — your normal speaking pitch.
Tone 6 · low and flat, just under tone 3.
Tone 1 · high, cut short by the -k.
Tone 6 · low, cut short by the -k. Same syllable as 識 (sik1)!
Tone 1 · high and flat.
Tone 3 · mid and flat, as in 鍾意 (zung1 ji3).
Tone 6 · low and flat.

units.title: About Me
units.desc: Say who you are, where you're from, where you live and what languages you speak

ex.en: We live in London.
Are you (all) French?
They aren't Swiss.

words.note: Place + 人 (jan4) = someone from there: 香港人 (hoeng1 gong2 jan4) a Hongkonger, 瑞士人 (seoi6 si6 jan4) a Swiss.

ex.en: I'm a Hongkonger.

words.note: 我叫 (ngo5 giu3) + name = My name is… / I'm called…

ex.en: He's called Ka-ming.

words.note: Said meng2 in everyday speech: 你叫咩名啊 (nei5 giu3 me1 meng2 aa3)？ (What's your name?). The more formal 名字 (ming4 zi6) keeps ming4.

ex.en: What's your name?

words.note: Polite opener before a question to a stranger.

ex.en: Excuse me, what's your name?

words.note: Literally 'fragrant harbour'.

ex.en: My family is in Hong Kong.

words.note: Literally 'come out into the world'. 喺 (hai2) + place + 出世 (ceot1 sai3) = be born in…

ex.en: I was born in Hong Kong.
I really like Switzerland.

words.note: A sound transliteration of 'Canada'. Add 人 (jan4) for the people: 加拿大人 (gaa1 naa4 daai6 jan4) = a Canadian.

ex.en: I'm a Canadian.
My big sister lives in France.

words.note: 國 (gwok3) = country: 中國 (zung1 gwok3) China, 英國 (jing1 gwok3) the UK, 美國 (mei5 gwok3) the USA.

ex.en: Where in London do you live?

words.note: 住喺 (zyu6 hai2) + place = live in. 喺 (hai2) is 'at / in'.

ex.en: Where do you live?

words.en: to know how to; to know (a person)
words.note: 識講 (sik1 gong2) = can speak. 我識佢 (ngo5 sik1 keoi5) = I know him.

ex.en: Do you know him?
What are you saying?

words.note: 話 (waa6) is waa2 here (tone change). Literally 'the speech of Guangdong'.

ex.en: Can you speak Cantonese?

words.note: Most languages end in 文 (man2), a tone change from man4: 英文 (jing1 man2), 法文 (faat3 man2), 中文 (zung1 man2). 講英文 (gong2 jing1 man2) = speak English. Dialects use 話 (waa2 here): 廣東話 (gwong2 dung1 waa2).

ex.en: My little sister doesn't speak English.
Is French difficult?
I speak a little Cantonese.

words.note: 我嘅 (ngo5 ge3) = my / mine, 佢嘅 (keoi5 ge3) = his / hers. For family it's usually left out: 我細佬 (ngo5 sai3 lou2) = my little brother.

ex.en: This computer is mine.

words.note: Goes BEFORE the verb, never at the end: 我都係 (ngo5 dou1 hai6) = me too.

ex.en: I'm a Canadian too.

words.note: Starts the second half of a sentence. Very often shortened to 但 (daan6).

ex.en: I speak English, but not French.

words.note: Same as 但係 (daan6 hai6), a little softer.

ex.en: Cantonese is hard, but I love it.

words.note: Starts a sentence that follows from what was just said: 噉你係香港人 (gam2 nei5 hai6 hoeng1 gong2 jan4)？ = So you're a Hongkonger?

ex.en: So where do you live?

words.note: 結咗婚 (git3 zo2 fan1) = married. 咗 (zo2) marks something done — more in Days & Time.

ex.en: Do you want to get married?

sentences.en: I'm from Hong Kong. And you?
I'm a Canadian, but I was born in Hong Kong.
We now live in Switzerland.
I can speak a little Cantonese.
Can she speak English?
Are they French?
No, they're Swiss.
What's his name?
Where were you born?
They're getting married in London.
Cantonese is hard, English isn't.
Do you (all) live in London?
My big sister lives in France too.

grammar.title: 係 (hai6) + place + 人 (jan4) = nationality
grammar.explain: Add 人 (jan4) after a place to say where someone is from: 香港人 (hoeng1 gong2 jan4), 瑞士人 (seoi6 si6 jan4), 法國人 (faat3 gwok3 jan4). To ask, put 邊度 (bin1 dou6) in the place slot: 你係邊度人啊 (nei5 hai6 bin1 dou6 jan4 aa3)？

grammar.title: 哋 (dei6) makes pronouns plural
grammar.explain: 我 (ngo5) → 我哋 (ngo5 dei6) (we), 你 (nei5) → 你哋 (nei5 dei6) (you all), 佢 (keoi5) → 佢哋 (keoi5 dei6) (they). Only pronouns take 哋 (dei6), not nouns.

examples.en: Do they live in Hong Kong?

grammar.title: 係 (hai6) 'is' vs 喺 (hai2) 'at'
grammar.explain: Two words, two tones: 係 (hai6) is low and flat and links two nouns; 喺 (hai2) rises and gives a place: 住喺倫敦 (zyu6 hai2 leon4 deon1) = live in London.

grammar.title: 嘅 (ge3) = 's
grammar.explain: Noun or pronoun + 嘅 (ge3) shows who owns something: 我嘅 (ngo5 ge3) mine, 家明嘅 (gaa1 ming4 ge3) Ka-ming's. With family and close friends, leave it out: 我細佬 (ngo5 sai3 lou2).

examples.en: My little brother's computer is very expensive.

grammar.title: 都 (dou1) goes before the verb
grammar.explain: English puts 'too' at the end; Cantonese puts 都 (dou1) right after the subject, before the verb.

grammar.title: But: 但係 (daan6 hai6) / 不過 (bat1 gwo3)
grammar.explain: Both mean 'but' and start the second half. 不過 (bat1 gwo3) is a touch softer; in quick speech 但係 (daan6 hai6) often becomes just 但 (daan6).

examples.en: I'm a Canadian, but I was born in Hong Kong.
He doesn't eat pork, but he eats beef.

lines.en: Hello! Did you just move in?
Yes, I'm Mark. I live next door to you.
I'm Yan. Wow, you speak Cantonese?
Just a little. I was born in Hong Kong.
So you're a Hongkonger?
I'm a Canadian, but my family are all Hongkongers.
Your Cantonese is really good!
Thanks! Do you speak French?
Not a word! You teach me!
Sure, no problem!

questions.q: Where does Mark live?
Where was Mark born?
What nationality is Mark?
What does Yan ask Mark to do?

card.title: A big rise and a small rise
card.explain: Both tones go up. Tone 2 starts mid and climbs high, like a surprised 'eh?'. Tone 5 starts low and rises only to the middle, a lazy shrug. You already say tone 5 in 我 (ngo5) and 你 (nei5).

items.note: Tone 2 · big rise, mid to high.
Tone 5 · small rise, low to mid.
Tone 2 · big rise.
Tone 5 · small rise.
Tone 2, a word you know: 我想 (ngo5 soeng2).
Tone 5 · small rise. You'll learn it as a word next unit.
Tone 6 · low and flat — not rising! Mix up 買 (maai5) and 賣 (maai6) and you buy instead of sell.

units.title: Numbers & Money
units.desc: Count, give phone numbers, ask prices and haggle at a market stall

ex.en: Boss, I'll take one.

words.note: Use 二 (ji6) when counting and in bigger numbers (十二 (sap6 ji6), 二十 (ji6 sap6)). Before a measure word, 'two' is 兩 (loeng5).

ex.en: One, two, three!
I have three little sisters.

words.note: Sounds like 死 (sei2, to die), so 4 is unlucky — many HK buildings skip the 4th floor.

ex.en: There are four of us.

words.note: A syllable with no vowel: just hum 'ng' with a low rising tone.

ex.en: This one is five dollars.
There are six people in my family.
Seven dollars each.

words.note: Lucky! It rhymes with 發 (faat3, to get rich).

ex.en: Eighty-eight dollars? That's cheap!

words.note: 九 (gau2) also sounds like 久 (gau2) (long-lasting) — another lucky number.

ex.en: It's ninety-nine dollars, not expensive.

words.note: Careful: 十 (sap6, ten) vs 四 (sei3, four). Keep the -p closed at the end of sap6.

ex.en: Three for ten dollars!

words.note: 一百五 (jat1 baak3 ng5) or just 百五 (baak3 ng5) = 150. A gap inside a number is filled with 零 (ling4) 'zero': 一百零五 (jat1 baak3 ling4 ng5) = 105.

ex.en: This one is 150 dollars.
Three thousand dollars? That's too expensive!

words.note: Chinese counts in 萬 (maan6) (10,000): 10,000 = 一萬 (jat1 maan6), 100,000 = 十萬 (sap6 maan6), 1,000,000 = 一百萬 (jat1 baak3 maan6).

ex.en: Ten thousand dollars? I don't want it!

words.note: 兩 (loeng5) + measure word: 兩個 (loeng5 go3), 兩張 (loeng5 zoeng1), 兩蚊 (loeng5 man1). Never 二個 (ji6 go3).

ex.en: I have two big sisters.

words.note: Numbers and 呢 (ni1)/嗰 (go2) need a measure word before a noun. 個 (go3) is the default one: 一個人 (jat1 go3 jan4), 呢個 (ni1 go3).

ex.en: I'll take this one.
How many do you want?

words.note: In speech it's cin2 (changed tone); the reading-aloud form is cin4. 幾多錢 (gei2 do1 cin2)？ = How much (money)? Shorter: 幾錢 (gei2 cin2).

ex.en: How much is this?

words.note: The spoken word for dollar. Written price tags say 元 (jyun4), but nobody says it.

ex.en: This one is twenty dollars.

words.note: Meaning 'cheap', it's always peng4 in speech. The reading ping4 means 'flat / peaceful', as in 和平 (wo4 ping4).

ex.en: This one isn't cheap, you know.
Is it expensive?

words.note: 咁平 (gam3 peng4)？ = That cheap?! Shows surprise. Don't confuse with 噉 (gam2) 'so / then'.

ex.en: That expensive?!

words.note: 好貴 (hou2 gwai3) = very expensive; 太貴 (taai3 gwai3) = too expensive. Usually ends with 喇 (laa3) or 啦 (laa1).

ex.en: That's too expensive!

words.note: Before a noun: 'the… / some…' (啲錢 (di1 cin2) = the money). After an adjective: 'a bit more' — 平啲 (peng4 di1) = a bit cheaper.

ex.en: Make it a bit cheaper, boss!

words.note: You know 買嘢 (maai5 je5) 'go shopping'. Careful: 賣 (maai6) with a low flat tone means 'to sell'!

ex.en: I want to buy a bike.

words.en: to want; to take (when buying); need to
words.note: 要 (jiu3) + thing: 'I'll take…' when buying or ordering. 要 (jiu3) + verb = need to. 唔要 (m4 jiu3) = I don't want it.

ex.en: I'll take three.

words.note: The friendly way to call a stallholder or shopkeeper, whatever their age. A woman owner is often 老闆娘 (lou5 baan2 noeng4).

ex.en: Boss, how much is this?

sentences.en: How much is this bicycle?
Three hundred dollars? So expensive!
It's not expensive, it's really cheap!
Boss, I'll take two.
There are four of us in my family.
My phone number is 9123 4567.
This one is $2.50.
How much is beef per catty?
Too expensive — make it a bit cheaper!
How many do you want to buy?
Two for me, please.
Things in Switzerland are so expensive!
How many computers do you have at home?

grammar.title: Building numbers 11–99
grammar.explain: Just stack them: 十一 (sap6 jat1) = 10+1, 二十 (ji6 sap6) = 2×10, 二十五 (ji6 sap6 ng5) = 25. In speech, 二十 (ji6 sap6) + digit is usually shortened to 廿 (jaa6): 廿五 (jaa6 ng5) = 25.

grammar.title: 兩 (loeng5) vs 二 (ji6)
grammar.explain: 'Two' of something (before a measure word like 個 (go3), 張 (zoeng1), 蚊 (man1)) is 兩 (loeng5). Inside bigger numbers and when counting, use 二 (ji6): 十二個 (sap6 ji6 go3), 二十蚊 (ji6 sap6 man1).

grammar.title: Saying prices the HK way
grammar.explain: With cents, drop 蚊 (man1) and say 個 (go3): 個半 (go3 bun3) = $1.50 (半 (bun3) = half), 三個二 (saam1 go3 ji6) = $3.20. With hundreds, drop the last zero: 百五 (baak3 ng5) = 150, 三百二 (saam1 baak3 ji6) = 320.

grammar.title: Very, too, a bit more: 好 (hou2) · 太 (taai3) · 啲 (di1)
grammar.explain: 好貴 (hou2 gwai3) = very expensive. 太貴 (taai3 gwai3) = too expensive. Adjective + 啲 (di1) = a bit more: 平啲 (peng4 di1) = a bit cheaper — the magic word at a market.

dialogue.title: Buying fruit at a market stall

lines.en: Boss, how much are the oranges?
Three for ten dollars.
That cheap? I'll take six.
Six, that's twenty. Want some apples too?
How much is an apple?
Eight dollars each.
Eight dollars? Too expensive! No thanks.
OK then, five for thirty. How's that?
OK! Fifty dollars altogether — here you go.
Thanks a lot!

questions.q: How much are the oranges?
How many oranges does A buy?
Why does A first say no to the apples?
How much does A pay in total?

card.title: Stopped syllables
card.explain: Syllables ending in -p, -t or -k are cut short: close your lips (-p), touch your tongue to your teeth (-t) or the back of your mouth (-k), but don't release a sound. They still have a tone: high (1), mid (3) or low (6).

items.note: High, cut short by -t.
High, cut short by -t. c ≈ 'ts'.
Mid, long aa, then -t.
Low, cut short by -k.
Low, lips close for -p. Don't let it slide into 四 (sei3)!
High version of 十 (sap6).
Mid, long aa, then -k.
Low version of 百 (baak3).

units.title: Family & People
units.desc: Talk about your family, greet relatives the HK way, and say what you have (or don't)

words.note: Adults often say 阿爸 (aa3 baa4) or the casual 老豆 (lou5 dau6).

ex.en: My dad lives in Hong Kong.

words.note: Also 阿媽 (aa3 maa1).

ex.en: My mum was born in Hong Kong.

words.note: The everyday word — not slangy at all.

ex.en: My husband doesn't eat lamb.
Is your wife Swiss?

words.note: Usually with 個 (go3): 我個仔 (ngo5 go3 zai2) = my son. Also a 'little' suffix: 男仔 (naam4 zai2) boy.

ex.en: My son is eight.

words.note: 'Daughter' is neoi2 (tone change): 我個女 (ngo5 go3 neoi2). 女 (neoi5) on its own means 'female'.

ex.en: Does your daughter speak French?

words.note: 幾多歲 (gei2 do1 seoi3) = how old? No verb needed: 佢八歲 (keoi5 baat3 seoi3) = he is eight.

ex.en: How old is your daughter?

words.note: Chinese has different words for each side of the family.

ex.en: Grandpa is ninety.
Grandma loves watching TV.
My grandpa doesn't speak English.

words.note: Also a polite way to address any elderly woman.

ex.en: Where does your grandma live?

words.note: Same as 哥哥 (go4 go1) but more casual. Also 'boss / dude' in slang.

ex.en: My big brother is married.

words.note: Kids also call any man of their parents' age 叔叔 (suk1 suk1). An adult calls an older man 阿叔 (aa3 suk1).

ex.en: My uncle lives in London.

words.note: Dad's younger sister is 姑姐 (gu1 ze1).

ex.en: Auntie loves fish.

words.note: Mum's side has its own words: 舅父 (kau5 fu2) uncle, 姨媽 (ji4 maa1) aunt.

ex.en: My uncle speaks French.

words.note: Mum's younger sister is 阿姨 (aa3 ji1).

ex.en: Auntie, long time no see!

words.en: auntie (mum's younger sister; any older woman)
words.fr: tata (sœur cadette de la mère ; dame plus âgée)
words.note: The polite, friendly way to address a woman of your parents' age — a shop assistant, a neighbour, a friend's mum.

ex.en: Thank you, auntie!

words.en: older male cousin (on mum's side or via an aunt)
words.note: 表 (biu2) cousins: 表哥 (biu2 go1), 表姐 (biu2 ze2) older female cousin. Cousins through dad's brothers are 堂 (tong4): 堂哥 (tong4 go1).

ex.en: My cousin is in Hong Kong.
He's my good friend.
Does she have a boyfriend?

words.note: Only for a romantic partner. A female friend is just 朋友 (pang4 jau5).

ex.en: My little brother's girlfriend is French.

words.note: The everyday word. 家庭 (gaa1 ting4) is more formal: 'the family unit'.

ex.en: My family are all in Hong Kong.

words.note: Polite and kind. A more casual word is 細路 (sai3 lou6).

ex.en: Do you have kids?

words.note: Goes before the noun: 好多人 (hou2 do1 jan4) = lots of people. 好多嘢 (hou2 do1 je5) = lots of things.

ex.en: There are lots of people in Hong Kong.

words.note: Literally 'very long, not seen'. The classic greeting when you visit family in Hong Kong.

ex.en: Wow, long time no see! How have you been?

words.note: Literally 'eaten rice yet?'. It's a warm 'how are you', not an invitation. Answer 食咗喇 (sik6 zo2 laa3) 'yes, I have' even if you haven't!

ex.en: Auntie, have you eaten?

sentences.en: How many people are there in your family?
Four: Dad, Mum, my big brother and me.
Do you have a girlfriend?
I have a son and a daughter.
My wife and I live in London.
My grandma is ninety and still loves shopping!
Is he your boyfriend?
No, he's my husband!
Dad doesn't have a car; he rides a bike.
My son likes playing video games, my daughter likes running.
My uncle and aunt both live in Hong Kong.
I have lots of Swiss friends.
Grandpa, Grandma, have you eaten?

grammar.title: Dad's side or Mum's side?
grammar.explain: Chinese has a different word for each relative. Dad's side: 爺爺 (je4 je2), 嫲嫲 (maa4 maa4), 叔叔 (suk1 suk1), 姑媽 (gu1 maa1). Mum's side: 公公 (gung4 gung1), 婆婆 (po4 po2), 舅父 (kau5 fu2), 姨媽 (ji4 maa1).

examples.en: She's my dad's big sister, so she's my aunt.
He's my mum's little brother, so he's my uncle.

grammar.title: 'My' without 嘅 (ge3)
grammar.explain: For family and close people, just put the pronoun in front: 我媽媽 (ngo5 maa4 maa1) (my mum), 你老公 (nei5 lou5 gung1) (your husband). For 仔 (zai2) and 女 (neoi2), add the measure word 個 (go3): 我個仔 (ngo5 go3 zai2), 佢個女 (keoi5 go3 neoi2).

grammar.title: …嚟㗎 (lai4 gaa3) to say who someone is
grammar.explain: 係 (hai6) + noun + 嚟㗎 (lai4 gaa3) means 'is (actually) a…' — used when explaining or correcting who someone is.

grammar.title: Greeting family the HK way
grammar.explain: Older relatives rarely say 你好 (nei5 hou2). Call them by their title first — 婆婆 (po4 po2)！ 姨媽 (ji4 maa1)！ — then use a warm set phrase like 好耐冇見 (hou2 noi6 mou5 gin3) or 食咗飯未啊 (sik6 zo2 faan6 mei6 aa3)？

lines.en: Wow, Ming! Long time no see! Have you eaten?
Auntie, long time no see! Yes, I have, thanks.
How have you been? Busy?
Pretty good. This is my wife — she's Swiss.
Hello! Do you speak Cantonese?
Just a little. Hello, auntie!
Well done! Do you have any kids?
Yes, a son and a daughter. Our son is eight, our daughter five.
How lovely! Your cousin has two kids too.
Really? Where is he now?
His whole family lives in France.

questions.q: How does the aunt greet Ming?
options: Long time no see, have you eaten?
Good morning, how much is it?

questions.q: Where is Ming's wife from?
How old is Ming's son?
Where does Ming's cousin live?

card.title: The bottom of your voice
card.explain: Three tones live low: tone 4 falls to the very bottom, tone 5 rises a little, tone 6 stays flat just under your normal pitch. 嫲嫲 (maa4 maa4) and 爺爺 (je4 je2) start on tone 4.

items.note: Tone 4 · low and falling.
Tone 5 · low with a small rise.
Tone 6 · low and flat.
Tone 4 — the same sound as 嫲 (maa4) in 嫲嫲 (maa4 maa4).
Tone 5 · small rise.
Tone 6 · low and flat.
Tone 4 · low and falling.
Tone 6 · low and flat, as in 夜晚 (je6 maan5).

units.title: Days & Time
units.desc: Tell the time, talk about today, tomorrow and yesterday, and handle a phone call

ex.en: What day is it today?

words.note: 聽 (teng1) is ting1 here (as 'listen' it's teng1). In fast speech it often sounds like 'tim1 jat6'.

ex.en: OK, see you tomorrow!

words.note: Also written 琴日 (kam4 jat6) — same word, two pronunciations.

ex.en: Where did you go yesterday?
What do you want to eat tonight?
She watches TV in the morning.

words.note: Lunchtime and early afternoon. 下晝 (haa6 zau3) = afternoon.

ex.en: Shall we go shopping this afternoon?
I don't eat at night.

words.note: Same as 星期 (sing1 kei4) but more casual: 禮拜一 (lai5 baai3 jat1) = Monday … 禮拜六 (lai5 baai3 luk6) = Saturday, and Sunday is 禮拜日 (lai5 baai3 jat6) — not 七 (cat1)!

ex.en: I'm going shopping on Saturday.

words.note: 下個 (haa6 go3) = next, 上個 (soeng6 go3) = last: 下個月 (haa6 go3 jyut6) next month, 上個禮拜 (soeng6 go3 lai5 baai3) last week.

ex.en: See you next week!
What time is it now?

words.note: Number + 點 (dim2): 三點 (saam1 dim2) = three o'clock. The full form 點鐘 (dim2 zung1) is less common. Two o'clock is 兩點 (loeng5 dim2).

ex.en: Let's meet at seven!

words.note: 七點半 (cat1 dim2 bun3) = 7:30.

ex.en: It's half past two.

words.note: 鐘 (zung1) here means 'hour': 一個鐘 (jat1 go3 zung1) = an hour, 兩個鐘 (loeng5 go3 zung1) = two hours.

ex.en: Half an hour? That's ages!
Give me five minutes!

words.note: 早啲 (zou2 di1) = a bit earlier.

ex.en: You're so early today!
Sorry, I'm late!

words.note: 遲 (ci4) = late; 遲啲 (ci4 di1) = later on.

ex.en: When are you going to Hong Kong?

words.note: Months are numbered: 一月 (jat1 jyut6) January … 十二月 (sap6 ji6 jyut6) December. 下個月 (haa6 go3 jyut6) = next month.

ex.en: I'm going to France next month.

words.note: 今年 (gam1 nin4) this year, but 舊年 (gau6 nin2) last year and 出年 (ceot1 nin2) next year (tone change).

ex.en: I've lived in Hong Kong for ten years.

words.note: Dates go big → small: 十一月四號 (sap6 jat1 jyut6 sei3 hou6) = 4 November.

ex.en: What's the date today?

words.note: Like 今日 (gam1 jat6) today and 今晚 (gam1 maan5) tonight: 今 (gam1) = this / now.

ex.en: My little brother is eight this year.

words.note: Verb + 咗 (zo2): 食咗 (sik6 zo2) = have eaten, 去咗 (heoi3 zo2) = went / has gone. Don't mix it up with 做 (zou6) 'to do'.

ex.en: He's gone to France.

words.note: Usually ends with 喇 (laa3): 已經三點喇 (ji5 ging1 saam1 dim2 laa3)！ = It's already three!

ex.en: I've already eaten.

words.note: On the phone it rises: wai2. Said flat (wai3), it's a blunt 'hey!' to get someone's attention.

ex.en: Hello? Who's calling?

words.note: 等我 (dang2 ngo5) = wait for me. 等等 (dang2 dang2) = wait a moment / hold on.

ex.en: Wait for me!

words.note: 聽日見 (ting1 jat6 gin3)！ = See you tomorrow! You know it from 一陣見 (jat1 zan6 gin3) and 好耐冇見 (hou2 noi6 mou5 gin3).

ex.en: I'm seeing him tonight.

sentences.en: Today is the 4th of November, a Wednesday.
What day is it tomorrow?
It's half past three now.
I'm going running tomorrow morning.
Are you home tonight?
Sorry, I'm ten minutes late.
It was raining yesterday morning, so I didn't go running.
We're going to Hong Kong next week!
I'm waiting for you!
When is your birthday?
I go to bed at eleven at night.
It's already twelve o'clock!
When shall we meet?
Where did you go yesterday?

grammar.title: Time comes before the verb
grammar.explain: Put 'when' right after the subject (or at the very start), never at the end: 我聽日去 (ngo5 ting1 jat6 heoi3) = I'm going tomorrow. Bigger units come first: 聽日朝早七點 (ting1 jat6 ziu1 zou2 cat1 dim2).

examples.en: I'm going to Hong Kong tomorrow.
Tomorrow morning at seven, I go running.

grammar.title: Telling the time: 點 (dim2), 半 (bun3), 個字 (go3 zi6)
grammar.explain: Hour + 點 (dim2): 三點 (saam1 dim2). Add 半 (bun3) for half past: 三點半 (saam1 dim2 bun3). For other times, say the number the minute hand points at; each number is 一個字 (jat1 go3 zi6), five minutes: 三點三 (saam1 dim2 saam1) = 3:15, 三點九 (saam1 dim2 gau2) = 3:45. Exact minutes use 分 (fan1): 三點十分 (saam1 dim2 sap6 fan1).

grammar.title: 咗 (zo2) done, 緊 (gan2) going on
grammar.explain: Right after the verb, 緊 (gan2) means it's happening now and 咗 (zo2) means it's done. No change to the verb itself.

grammar.title: 喇 (laa3): something has changed
grammar.explain: At the end of a sentence, 喇 (laa3) says the situation is new: it's now late, you've now decided, it's now done.

grammar.title: On the phone
grammar.explain: Pick up with 喂 (wai2)？ A caller asks for someone with 搵 (wan2) 'look for'. Hold on = 等等 (dang2 dang2). Wrong number = 打錯 (daa2 co3). Can't hear = 聽唔到 (teng1 m4 dou2).

examples.en: Hello, who would you like to speak to?
Sorry, you've got the wrong number.

lines.en: Hello? Where are you? It's already half past three!
Sorry! I just got up.
What? It's the afternoon!
I only went to bed at two last night…
So what time will you get here?
Twenty minutes… no, half an hour!
Fine, I'll wait half an hour. See you at four!
Thanks! Dinner's on me tonight!

questions.q: What time is it when A calls?
Why is B late?
When will they meet?
How does B make up for it?

units.title: Food & Yum Cha
units.desc: Order dim sum and cha chaan teng classics, ask for the bill, and say what you like to eat and drink

words.note: 食 (sik6) = eat, 飲 (jam2) = drink. Soup is drunk too: 飲湯 (jam2 tong1).

ex.en: What would you like to drink?

words.note: 食飯 (sik6 faan6) = have a meal, not only rice. Uncooked rice is 米 (mai5).

ex.en: He ate two bowls of rice.
I'm having noodles for lunch.

words.note: At yum cha the classic is 普洱 (pou2 lei2), pu'er tea.

ex.en: My mum loves drinking tea.

words.en: to go for yum cha (dim sum)
words.fr: aller manger des dim sum (yum cha)
words.note: Literally 'drink tea', but it means the whole dim sum meal, usually in a 茶樓 (caa4 lau4).

ex.en: On Saturday we're going for dim sum together.
I need a coffee in the morning.
A glass of water, please.

words.note: For drinks say 好飲 (hou2 jam2). 'Really tasty' = 好好食 (hou2 hou2 sik6).

ex.en: The dim sum here is really good!

words.note: Measure word 間 (gaan1): 呢間餐廳 (ni1 gaan1 caan1 teng1) = this restaurant.

ex.en: This restaurant is expensive.
What dim sum do you like?

words.note: Classics: 蝦餃 (haa1 gaau2), 燒賣 (siu1 maai2), 叉燒包 (caa1 siu1 baau1) BBQ pork bun.

ex.en: I really like har gow.

words.note: Tone change: 賣 (maai6) 'sell' becomes maai2 in 燒賣 (siu1 maai2).

ex.en: There's pork in siu mai, you know.

words.note: Green vegetables are often 青菜 (ceng1 coi3); the classic one is 菜心 (coi3 sam1).

ex.en: You should eat more vegetables.

words.note: 肚 (tou5) = belly. To ask: 你肚唔肚餓啊 (nei5 tou5 m4 tou5 ngo6 aa3)？

ex.en: Are you hungry?

words.note: 食飽 (sik6 baau2) = to have eaten your fill.

ex.en: I'm really full, I won't eat any more.

words.note: Goes before the verb: 一齊食 (jat1 cai4 sik6), 一齊去 (jat1 cai4 heoi3).

ex.en: Let's eat together!

words.note: 'I can't eat spicy food' = 我唔食得辣 (ngo5 m4 sik6 dak1 laat6).

ex.en: This one is really spicy!

words.note: To get the bill, catch a waiter's eye and say 唔該 (m4 goi1), 埋單 (maai4 daan1)!

ex.en: We're full — let's get the bill.

words.note: Fills the 'something' slot: 食嘢 (sik6 je5) eat something, 飲嘢 (jam2 je5) have a drink, 嘢食 (je5 sik6) food.

ex.en: What would you like to eat?

words.note: Before a verb: 未食 (mei6 sik6) = haven't eaten yet. At the end of a question it means 'yet?': 食咗未 (sik6 zo2 mei6)？ = have you eaten yet?

ex.en: I haven't eaten yet.

words.note: Only for choices in a question. In statements 'or' is 或者 (waak6 ze2).

ex.en: Would you like tea or coffee?

words.note: 得唔得 (dak1 m4 dak1)？ = Is that OK? Answer 得 (dak1) (yes) or 唔得 (m4 dak1) (no). After a verb it means 'can': 食得 (sik6 dak1) = can eat.

ex.en: Can I have it without ice?

words.note: Cheap, fast and loud: milk tea, macaroni soup, pineapple buns. People often call it 茶記 (caa4 gei3).

ex.en: I love going to cha chaan tengs.

words.note: Strong black tea with evaporated milk. Iced: 凍奶茶 (dung3 naai5 caa4); hot: 熱奶茶 (jit6 naai5 caa4).

ex.en: The milk tea at cha chaan tengs is so good!

words.note: At the counter, 'to take away' is also 拎走 (ling1 zau2); eating in is 堂食 (tong4 sik6).

ex.en: Takeaway, please.

words.note: 走 (zau2) means 'leave out': 走甜 (zau2 tim4) = no sugar. 凍奶茶走冰 (dung3 naai5 caa4 zau2 bing1) = iced milk tea without ice cubes (chilled, not watered down).

ex.en: Milk tea, no ice, please.

sentences.en: I'm so hungry! Let's go and eat.
Shall we go for dim sum together?
I can't eat spicy food.
A basket of siu mai, please.
Food at cha chaan tengs is cheap.
I like noodles, I don't like rice.
Excuse me, the bill please!
I don't drink coffee — water's fine for me.
Do you want noodles or rice?
I still haven't eaten, I'm starving.
I'm full, thanks!
Let's order takeaway tonight.
This is too spicy, I'm not eating any more.

grammar.title: Ordering: 唔該 (m4 goi1) + 要 (jiu3) …
grammar.explain: Catch the staff's attention with 唔該 (m4 goi1)!, then say 要 (jiu3) + number + measure word + food. 畀 (bei2) … 我 (ngo5) 'give me …' works too.

examples.en: Excuse me, two baskets of har gow please.
I'll have a bowl of noodles.

grammar.title: Measure words for food
grammar.explain: Food is counted by its container: 籠 (lung4) steamer basket, 碗 (wun2) bowl, 杯 (bui1) cup / glass, 碟 (dip6) plate, 壺 (wu4) pot. For 'one', 一 (jat1) is often dropped: 要碗麵 (jiu3 wun2 min6).

examples.en: Let's get a plate of greens.

grammar.title: …咗 (zo2) … 未 (mei6)? Have you … yet?
grammar.explain: Verb + 咗 (zo2) + thing + 未 (mei6) asks 'have you done it yet?'. 食咗飯未啊 (sik6 zo2 faan6 mei6 aa3)？ is also the everyday greeting you met in Family. Answer 食咗喇 (sik6 zo2 laa3) (yes) or 未啊 (mei6 aa3) (not yet).

grammar.title: Or: 定係 (ding6 hai6) vs 或者 (waak6 ze2)
grammar.explain: In a question that offers a choice, 'or' is 定係 (ding6 hai6). In a statement — 'either is fine', 'maybe this or that' — use 或者 (waak6 ze2).

examples.en: Do you want tea or coffee?
Tea or coffee, either is fine.

lines.en: I'm starving! Let's order.
OK. Excuse me — a pot of pu'er and two baskets of har gow!
I want siu mai too! I love siu mai.
Wow, the har gow here is really good!
Huh? Where's the har gow? Did you eat it all?
Yes, sorry! I was really hungry.
Never mind, let's order another basket.
Are you full yet?
Full! Excuse me, the bill please!
It's on me today — I ate your har gow!

questions.q: What do they order first?
options: A pot of pu'er and two baskets of har gow
Two coffees and a bowl of noodles
A pot of pu'er and two baskets of siu mai
Water and a plate of vegetables

questions.q: What does A love to eat?
What happened to the har gow?
Who pays the bill, and why?
options: B, because B ate A's har gow
B, because A forgot the money

card.title: How people really say it
card.explain: Many Hongkongers, especially family at home, change a few sounds: n- becomes l- (你 (nei5) sounds like 'lei5'), ng- is dropped (我 (ngo5) sounds like 'o5'), gw- becomes g- (廣 (gwong2) sounds like 'gong2'). Some words also take a changed tone in speech: 名 (meng2), 錢 (cin2). Understand both; say whichever feels natural.

items.note: Short a — quick and tight. Compare 街 (gaai1).
Long aa — open your mouth wide and hold it.
Short a, like the u in English 'sun'.
Long aa, like 'a' in 'father'.
eo ≈ the 'eu' in French 'peur', gliding to a short i.
oe ≈ French 'eu' in 'heure'. c = 'ts' with a puff of air.
yu ≈ French 'u' in 'tu'.
ng- at the start, like the end of 'sing'. Many people just say 'o5'.

units.title: Getting Around
units.desc: Take the MTR, bus, minibus or taxi, ask the way and say where you are

words.note: Also heard as lei4. The opposite of 去 (heoi3).

ex.en: My friend is coming to Hong Kong tomorrow.

words.en: to go back / return (to a usual place)
words.note: Used for places you belong to: 返屋企 (faan1 uk1 kei2) go home, 返香港 (faan1 hoeng1 gong2) go back to HK.

ex.en: She's gone back to Hong Kong.

words.note: 坐 (co5) also works: 坐巴士 (co5 baa1 si2). 坐 (co5) alone = to sit.

ex.en: I take the MTR home.

words.note: Before a verb, 點 (dim2) = how: 點去 (dim2 heoi3) how to get there, 點講 (dim2 gong2) how to say it. Same 點 (dim2) as in 點樣 (dim2 joeng2) and 點解 (dim2 gaai2).

ex.en: How do I get to your place?

words.note: Official name: 港鐵 (gong2 tit3), the MTR. People say both 搭地鐵 (daap3 dei6 tit3) and 搭港鐵 (daap3 gong2 tit3).

ex.en: Where is the MTR station?

words.note: From English 'bus'. Bus stop = 巴士站 (baa1 si2 zaam6).

ex.en: Let's take the bus.
Taking a taxi is expensive.

words.note: The red or green minibuses (up to 19 seats). Shout 有落 (jau5 lok6) ('getting off!') to the driver before your stop.

ex.en: Is there a minibus to the airport?

words.note: 地鐵站 (dei6 tit3 zaam6) MTR station, 巴士站 (baa1 si2 zaam6) bus stop, 下個站 (haa6 go3 zaam6) next stop.

ex.en: I'm getting off at the next stop.
Which exit should I take?

words.note: 轉左 (zyun3 zo2) = turn left. On the left = 喺左邊 (hai2 zo2 bin1).

ex.en: Turn left there.

words.note: 轉右 (zyun3 jau6) = turn right. On the right = 喺右邊 (hai2 jau6 bin1). 左右 (zo2 jau2) after a number = 'about'.

ex.en: Turn right at the junction.

words.note: 轉左 (zyun3 zo2) turn left, 轉右 (zyun3 jau6) turn right, 轉車 (zyun3 ce1) change trains/buses.

ex.en: Change trains at Central.
Straight ahead, please. (to a taxi driver)

words.note: 呢度 (ni1 dou6) here, 嗰度 (go2 dou6) there. Usually with 喺 (hai2): 我喺呢度 (ngo5 hai2 ni1 dou6) I'm here.

ex.en: I'm here!

words.note: 嗰 (go2) = that, so 嗰度 (go2 dou6) is 'that place'.

ex.en: There's a bus stop there.

words.note: On its own it's kan5: 好近 (hou2 kan5) = very close. In compounds it's gan6: 附近 (fu6 gan6) = nearby.

ex.en: The MTR station is very close.
Is it far?

words.note: Answer with a duration: 十分鐘 (sap6 fan1 zung1), 半個鐘 (bun3 go3 zung1). Add 左右 (zo2 jau2) for 'about'.

ex.en: How long do you have to wait?

words.note: 到咗 (dou3 zo2) = has arrived. 就到 (zau6 dou3) = almost there.

ex.en: I've arrived!

words.note: Get on = 上車 (soeng5 ce1).

ex.en: Where do we get off?

words.note: Plane = 飛機 (fei1 gei1).

ex.en: How long does it take to get to the airport?

words.en: (after a verb) have ever done; have been to
words.note: Experience: 去過 (heoi3 gwo3) = have been to. Ask 有冇 (jau5 mou5) + verb + 過 (gwo3)? Answer 去過 (heoi3 gwo3), 未去過 (mei6 heoi3 gwo3) (not yet) or 冇去過 (mou5 heoi3 gwo3) (never).

ex.en: Have you ever taken a minibus?

words.en: no need to; don't have to
words.note: 唔使 (m4 sai2) + verb = no need to. To ask: 使唔使 (sai2 m4 sai2) + verb? It's also inside 唔使唔該 (m4 sai2 m4 goi1) 'no need to thank me'.

ex.en: No need to change.

sentences.en: Excuse me, how do I get to Central?
Go straight, and turn left at the junction.
The MTR station is close, it's only a five-minute walk.
It takes about forty minutes by bus.
Is Tsim Sha Tsui far from here?
Where are you? — I'm at the bus stop.
To the airport, please. (to a taxi driver)
I walk home.
Do I need to change? — No need.
The airport isn't far, it's about half an hour.
What time do you get to the airport?
Come to my place on Saturday!
Have you been to Hong Kong yet? — Yes, I have.
There's no MTR station there, you have to take a taxi.

grammar.title: No 'to': just verb + place
grammar.explain: 去 (heoi3), 嚟 (lai4) and 返 (faan1) take the place directly, with no word for 'to'. To say how you travel, put 搭 (daap3) + transport first.

examples.en: I take the MTR to the airport.

grammar.title: Place + 點去 (dim2 heoi3)? How do I get there?
grammar.explain: Say the place first, then 點去 (dim2 heoi3): 機場點去啊 (gei1 coeng4 dim2 heoi3 aa3)？ 'How do I get to the airport?' 點 (dim2) + any verb asks 'how': 點講 (dim2 gong2) 'how do you say it'.

examples.en: How do I get to the MTR station?
How do you say this in Cantonese?

grammar.title: 喺 (hai2) + 呢度 (ni1 dou6) / 嗰度 (go2 dou6) before the verb
grammar.explain: 'Where' goes before the action, not at the end like in English: 我喺嗰度等 (ngo5 hai2 go2 dou6 dang2) is literally 'I at there wait'.

grammar.title: How long? 要幾耐 (jiu3 gei2 noi6)
grammar.explain: Ask 'how long does it take' with 要幾耐 (jiu3 gei2 noi6). Answer with 要 (jiu3) + duration; add 左右 (zo2 jau2) after it for 'about'.

examples.en: How long does it take to walk there?

grammar.title: Verb + 過 (gwo3) = have ever done
grammar.explain: 過 (gwo3) straight after the verb means you've done it at some point in your life. 未 (mei6) + verb + 過 (gwo3) = haven't yet; 冇 (mou5) + verb + 過 (gwo3) = never have.

examples.en: I've been to Hong Kong, but not to London yet.
Have you ever had har gow?

grammar.title: 唔使 (m4 sai2) = no need
grammar.explain: 唔使 (m4 sai2) + verb = there's no need to. Ask with 使唔使 (sai2 m4 sai2) + verb? and answer 唔使 (m4 sai2) or 要 (jiu3).

examples.en: No need to wait for me.
Do we need a taxi? — No, it's very close.

dialogue.title: Asking the way to the MTR

lines.en: Excuse me, how do I get to the MTR station?
Go straight, and turn right at the junction.
Is it far?
Not far, about five minutes on foot.
Actually I'm going to the airport. What should I take?
Take the airport bus, it's very convenient. The stop is over there.
Do I need to change?
No, you'll be there in about an hour.
Thanks so much!
No problem.

questions.q: Where should A turn to reach the MTR station?
How far is the MTR station on foot?
What does B suggest for getting to the airport?
Does A need to change on the way to the airport?

units.title: Shopping
units.desc: Point at things, ask for sizes and colours, pay, bargain at the market and ask for help

words.note: 呢 (ni1) + classifier: 呢件衫 (ni1 gin6 saam1) this top. Plural: 呢啲 (ni1 di1) these, no classifier needed.

ex.en: How much is this?

words.note: 嗰 (go2) = that. 嗰件 (go2 gin6) that top, 嗰啲 (go2 di1) those.

ex.en: I want that one, not this one.

words.note: 一件衫 (jat1 gin6 saam1) a top. Trousers take 條 (tiu4), shoes come in a pair: 對 (deoi3).

ex.en: How much is this one?

words.note: Classifier 件 (gin6): 一件衫 (jat1 gin6 saam1). Clothes in general = 衫 (saam1) too.

ex.en: I want to buy a top.

words.note: For people, clothes, views, even fish at the market. 靚仔 (leng3 zai2) handsome guy, 靚女 (leng3 neoi2) pretty girl: stallholders call every customer that!

ex.en: This top is really pretty!

words.note: 試下 (si3 haa5) = have a try: 下 (haa5) after a verb means 'a bit, briefly' (睇下 (tai2 haa5) have a look). Fitting room = 試身室 (si3 san1 sat1).

ex.en: Go on, try it!
These shoes are too big.

words.note: Sizes: 細碼 (sai3 maa5) S, 中碼 (zung1 maa5) M, 大碼 (daai6 maa5) L.

ex.en: This top is a bit small.

words.note: Classifier 條 (tiu4): 一條褲 (jat1 tiu4 fu3). Jeans = 牛仔褲 (ngau4 zai2 fu3).

ex.en: These trousers are really nice.

words.note: Classifier 對 (deoi3, a pair). Trainers = 波鞋 (bo1 haai4).

ex.en: I like that pair of shoes.
Do you have other colours?

words.note: Red is the lucky colour, especially at Chinese New Year. Others: 黑色 (hak1 sik1) black, 白色 (baak6 sik1) white, 藍色 (laam4 sik1) blue.

ex.en: My mum likes red.

words.note: 平啲啦 (peng4 di1 laa1)！ = come on, a bit cheaper! The classic market-stall line.

ex.en: Can you make it cheaper?

words.note: After a verb: 食多啲 (sik6 do1 di1) eat more, 買多啲 (maai5 do1 di1) buy more. Opposite: 少啲 (siu2 di1) less.

ex.en: I want to buy more clothes.

words.en: on sale; to reduce the price

ex.en: These clothes are on sale, really cheap!

words.note: Also written 俾錢 (bei2 cin2). 'I'll pay' = 我畀 (ngo5 bei2).

ex.en: Where do I pay?

words.note: Many market stalls take cash only: 淨係收現金 (zing6 hai6 sau1 jin6 gam1).

ex.en: I don't have any cash.

words.en: to pay by card (swipe a card)
words.note: 碌 (luk1) = to swipe; 卡 (kaat1) comes from English 'card'. Contactless: 拍卡 (paak3 kaat1) = tap your card.

ex.en: I'd like to pay by card.

words.note: HK's stored-value card for the MTR, buses, shops. Top up = 增值 (zang1 zik6).

ex.en: Do you take Octopus?

words.note: Literally 'money bag'. A handbag is 手袋 (sau2 doi2).

ex.en: Where's my wallet?

words.note: Goes before the verb: 淨係睇下 (zing6 hai6 tai2 haa5) just looking. 淨係有 (zing6 hai6 jau5) + amount = only have …

ex.en: Just looking, thanks.

words.note: Wet market: fresh meat, fish and vegetables. A supermarket is 超市 (ciu1 si5). Grocery shopping for dinner = 買餸 (maai5 sung3).

ex.en: The vegetables at the market are very fresh.

words.note: 唔夠錢 (m4 gau3 cin2) = not enough money. 夠唔夠 (gau3 m4 gau3) = is it enough?

ex.en: I don't have enough money.

words.note: The yes/no form of 可以 (ho2 ji5). The polite way to ask for permission or a favour. Answer 可以 (ho2 ji5) or 唔可以 (m4 ho2 ji5).

ex.en: Can I try it on?

words.en: to help; to do something for someone
words.note: 幫 (bong1) + person + verb = do it for them: 幫我睇下 (bong1 ngo5 tai2 haa5) have a look for me. 'Can you help me?' = 可唔可以幫我啊 (ho2 m4 ho2 ji5 bong1 ngo5 aa3)？

ex.en: Excuse me, could you help me?

words.note: Only for real emergencies (literally 'save life'). To ask a favour, use 可唔可以幫我啊 (ho2 m4 ho2 ji5 bong1 ngo5 aa3)？ instead. Emergency number in Hong Kong: 999.

ex.en: Help!

sentences.en: Boss, how much is this top? (老闆 (lou5 baan2) is how you address any shopkeeper)
Do you have a bigger one?
This one is too expensive, that one is cheaper.
Do you have these trousers in red?
I'll take two of these.
Is a hundred dollars enough?
I don't have cash, can I pay with Octopus?
This red one is really pretty!
There's a big sale here today.
My grandma loves going to the wet market to buy vegetables.
I don't need a bag, thanks.
These shoes are too small, do you have a bigger size?
Who's paying? — I'll pay!
I only have a hundred dollars.

grammar.title: 呢 (ni1) / 嗰 (go2) + classifier + noun
grammar.explain: 'This' and 'that' need a classifier between them and the noun: 呢件衫 (ni1 gin6 saam1) this top, 嗰條褲 (go2 tiu4 fu3) those trousers, 呢對鞋 (ni1 deoi3 haai4) this pair of shoes. For plurals use 啲 (di1): 呢啲衫 (ni1 di1 saam1) these clothes.

examples.en: That pair of shoes is cheap.

grammar.title: Adjective + 啲 (di1) = a bit more
grammar.explain: Put 啲 (di1) after an adjective to mean '-er / a bit more': 平啲 (peng4 di1) cheaper, 大啲 (daai6 di1) bigger, 細啲 (sai3 di1) smaller. After a verb, 多啲 (do1 di1) = more: 買多啲 (maai5 do1 di1) buy more.

examples.en: Do you have a smaller one?

grammar.title: 淨係 (zing6 hai6) = only
grammar.explain: 淨係 (zing6 hai6) goes before the verb, never at the end: 我淨係有現金 (ngo5 zing6 hai6 jau5 jin6 gam1) = I only have cash.

grammar.title: Asking for help: 可唔可以 (ho2 m4 ho2 ji5) + 幫 (bong1)
grammar.explain: 可唔可以 (ho2 m4 ho2 ji5) + verb asks politely: 'can I…?' or 'could you…?'. Add 幫我 (bong1 ngo5) for 'for me'. Start with 唔該 (m4 goi1) to get someone's attention.

examples.en: Excuse me, could you have a look for me?

lines.en: Boss, how much is this bag?
Three hundred dollars. It's really nice!
Wow, so expensive! Can you go cheaper?
OK, two hundred and eighty.
Two hundred, come on. OK?
No way… two fifty, that's already really cheap.
Hmm… do you have it in red?
Yes! Here, have a look.
OK. Do you take Octopus?
No, cash only!
Oh no, I only have two hundred dollars in my wallet…
Fine, fine, two hundred. It's yours!

questions.q: What was the first price?
Which colour does A ask for?
How does A have to pay?
What price do they finally agree on, and why?
options: $200, because that's all A has in the wallet
$250, the lowest price B will accept
$300, because A wants the red one

units.title: My Day
units.desc: Describe your daily routine and put actions in order: first, then, still, again

words.note: Also 'to wake up' in everyday speech. Alarm clock = 鬧鐘 (naau6 zung1).

ex.en: What time do you get up?

words.note: Careful: 刷 (caat3) starts with c-, not s-. Toothbrush = 牙刷 (ngaa4 caat2).

ex.en: Go brush your teeth!

words.note: Literally 'rinse cool'. Hongkongers usually shower at night.

ex.en: I'm in the shower, hang on!
I usually have breakfast at a cha chaan teng.

words.en: to leave the house, go out
words.note: Literally 'go out the door'. 出街 (ceot1 gaai1) = go out (into town, to eat or shop).

ex.en: I leave the house at eight every day.

words.note: 返 (faan1) again: work is a place you 'return' to every day.

ex.en: I take the MTR to work.

words.note: 收工 (sau1 gung1) is also common, and is used as a cheerful 'done for the day!'

ex.en: What time do you finish work?

words.note: Finish school = 放學 (fong3 hok6).

ex.en: My son goes to school at eight.

words.note: Very HK. 晏 (aan3) = midday (晏晝 (aan3 zau3)).

ex.en: Shall we have lunch together?
Come to my place for dinner tonight.

words.note: Literally 'cook rice', but means cooking any meal.

ex.en: Who cooks at your home?
I cook, you wash the dishes.
I do the laundry on Sundays.

words.note: 執 (zap1) = pick up / tidy. 執嘢 (zap1 je5) = pack your things.

ex.en: My place is so messy, I need to tidy up.

words.note: 日日 (jat6 jat6) means the same and is very colloquial.

ex.en: I go running every day.

words.note: 平時 (ping4 si4) 'normally' is used the same way.

ex.en: I usually get up at seven.

words.note: Before the verb: 你先食 (nei5 sin1 sik6) you eat first. Very Cantonese at the end of a sentence too: 你食先 (nei5 sik6 sin1) same meaning.

ex.en: You eat first.

words.note: Pairs with 先 (sin1): 先 (sin1) A 再 (zoi3) B = first A, then B. Also 'again' for the future: 再見 (zoi3 gin3) see you again.

ex.en: Come again tomorrow!
I brush my teeth, then I shower.

words.note: Verb + 完 (jyun4) + 之後 (zi1 hau6) = after doing: 食完飯之後 (sik6 jyun4 faan6 zi1 hau6).

ex.en: After work I go to the gym.

words.note: 食完 (sik6 jyun4) finish eating, 做完 (zou6 jyun4) finish doing, 洗完 (sai2 jyun4) finish washing.

ex.en: Have you finished eating?

words.note: 一個鐘頭 (jat1 go3 zung1 tau4) = one hour; often shortened to 一個鐘 (jat1 go3 zung1).

ex.en: I work nine hours a day.

words.note: 仲 (zung6) + verb = still: 仲瞓緊覺 (zung6 fan3 gan2 gaau3) still asleep. 仲未 (zung6 mei6) = still not yet. 仲 (zung6) + adjective = even more: 仲貴 (zung6 gwai3).

ex.en: He still hasn't got up.

words.note: For something that has happened again, often with annoyance. For 'again' in the future, use 再 (zoi3).

ex.en: You're late again!

words.en: then, right after; (as soon as … ) then
words.note: A 就 (zau6) B = once A is done, B follows straight away. 就 (zau6) goes before the second verb, after the subject.

ex.en: I'll leave as soon as I've eaten.

words.note: 我自己 (ngo5 zi6 gei2) myself, 你自己 (nei5 zi6 gei2) yourself. Before a verb: do it yourself.

ex.en: I usually cook for myself.

sentences.en: I get up at seven every day.
First brush your teeth, then have breakfast.
I usually have lunch at one.
After work I go to the market, then I go home and cook.
It takes me an hour to get to work.
I don't have to go to work on Saturdays.
Do you shower in the morning or at night?
My husband washes the dishes after dinner.
On Sundays I tidy up and do the laundry.
The kids finish school at three-thirty.
I have to get up very early tomorrow, so I want to go to bed early tonight.
He's still not up, he's going to be late again!
I live alone, so I usually cook for myself.
You eat first, I'm not hungry yet.

grammar.title: Ordering actions: 先 (sin1)…再 (zoi3)…, 然後 (jin4 hau6), 之後 (zi1 hau6)
grammar.explain: 先 (sin1) A 再 (zoi3) B = first A, then B (often an instruction). 然後 (jin4 hau6) links a list of steps. X 之後 (zi1 hau6) = after X; use verb + 完 (jyun4) + 之後 (zi1 hau6) for 'after finishing'.

examples.en: Wash your hands first, then eat.
I get up, brush my teeth, then shower.

grammar.title: 仲 (zung6) = still
grammar.explain: 仲 (zung6) before a verb means the situation hasn't changed yet. 仲未 (zung6 mei6) = still not (yet), the classic answer to '…未 (mei6)?' questions.

examples.en: Have you had lunch yet? — Not yet.

grammar.title: 又 (jau6) or 再 (zoi3)? Two kinds of 'again'
grammar.explain: 又 (jau6) = it has happened again (past or now, often a complaint). 再 (zoi3) = do it again later (future, requests, plans).

grammar.title: A 就 (zau6) B = as soon as A, then B
grammar.explain: 就 (zau6) links two actions that follow each other straight away. It goes right before the second verb.

examples.en: I go home as soon as I finish work.
Go to bed as soon as you get home.

grammar.title: Duration goes after the verb
grammar.explain: 'For how long' comes after the verb: 等咗半個鐘 (dang2 zo2 bun3 go3 zung1) waited for half an hour. Clock time ('at seven') comes before the verb.

examples.en: I waited for half an hour.
He works ten hours a day.

lines.en: Hey! It's already eight-thirty, and you're still not up?
What?! My alarm didn't ring!
Don't you start work at nine?
Yes! It takes me forty minutes to get there. I'm going to be late again!
Brush your teeth first, then go. Skip the shower.
What about breakfast?
Here's a pineapple bun, eat it on the way.
Thanks! I'll cook dinner tonight!
Deal. Then I'll do the dishes once we've eaten.

questions.q: What time is it when A wakes B?
Why did B oversleep?
What does A say B can skip?
Who will do what tonight?
options: B cooks, A washes the dishes
A cooks, B washes the dishes

units.title: Making Plans
units.desc: Suggest plans, fix a time and place, reschedule, and explain why you're running late

words.en: to arrange to meet; an appointment
words.note: 我約咗人 (ngo5 joek3 zo2 jan4) = I'm meeting someone. 有約 (jau5 joek3) = I have plans.

ex.en: I've arranged to meet a friend for dinner on Friday.

words.note: Other words can go inside it: 見過面 (gin3 gwo3 min6) have met, 見一次面 (gin3 jat1 ci3 min6) meet once.

ex.en: We haven't met up in ages!

words.note: Question form: 得唔得閒 (dak1 m4 dak1 haan4)? 'Are you free?' 有空 (jau5 hung1) means the same but sounds more formal.

ex.en: Are you free on Saturday?

words.note: Same meaning as 得閒 (dak1 haan4), which is the more colloquial everyday word; 有空 (jau5 hung1) sounds a bit more formal.

ex.en: When are you free next week?

words.note: 不如 (bat1 jyu4) … 啦 (laa1) is the standard way to suggest something.

ex.en: How about we go and eat hotpot?
Good idea! I haven't been in ages.

words.en: is that OK? / does that work?
words.note: Answer 得 (dak1) (OK) or 唔得 (m4 dak1) (no, can't).

ex.en: Seven-thirty, does that work for you?
He's never on time.
Can we make it a bit earlier?
I can't today — let's arrange it another time.

words.en: in a moment; a little while
words.note: 一陣見 (jat1 zan6 gin3) = see you in a bit. 等一陣 (dang2 jat1 zan6) = wait a moment.

ex.en: OK, see you in a bit!
It's raining, we cancelled our plans.
Can we reschedule to next week?
Sorry, something came up at the last minute, I can't come.

words.note: 記得 (gei3 dak1) + verb = remember to do.

ex.en: Remember to call me!

words.note: 唔記得咗 (m4 gei3 dak1 zo2) = have forgotten.

ex.en: Oops, I forgot we had plans today!

words.note: 打電話畀我 (daa2 din6 waa2 bei2 ngo5) = call me.

ex.en: Call me when you get there.

words.note: 傳訊息 (cyun4 seon3 sik1) = send a message. In real life most people just say the English 'WhatsApp'.

ex.en: I sent you a message — have you read it?
Why haven't you replied to me?

words.note: 我就嚟到 (ngo5 zau6 lai4 dou3) = I'm almost there. 就嚟 (zau6 lai4) + verb = about to.

ex.en: Hang on, I'm almost there!
Let's meet at the cinema entrance.

words.note: 傾偈 (king1 gai2) = to have a chat. 遲啲再傾 (ci4 di1 zoi3 king1) = let's talk later.

ex.en: Let's go for a coffee and have a proper chat.

words.en: to have something on; something came up
words.note: 臨時有事 (lam4 si4 jau5 si6) = something came up at the last minute. 冇事 (mou5 si6) = it's fine, nothing's wrong.

ex.en: I've got something on tomorrow, can we change the day?

sentences.en: Are you free tonight? How about going for dinner?
What time shall we meet, and where?
Dinner is at eight, let's meet at seven-thirty at the MTR station.
Sorry, I have to work overtime tonight — can we reschedule?
It's raining — let's reschedule.
He's late again — we've been waiting for half an hour!
Send me a message once you've left home.
Sorry, I forgot to call you.
Is Saturday afternoon OK? — No, I already have plans.
Let's meet up for a meal again some other time.
Wait for me a moment, I'm just coming down.
Why don't we go a bit earlier, there are fewer people.
Did he reply to you? — Not yet.

grammar.title: 不如 (bat1 jyu4)…啦 (laa1) = how about…
grammar.explain: Start with 不如 (bat1 jyu4) and end with 啦 (laa1) to make a friendly suggestion. To accept: 好啊 (hou2 aa3) / 好主意 (hou2 zyu2 ji3); to decline politely: 唔得啊 (m4 dak1 aa3)，我約咗人 (ngo5 joek3 zo2 jan4).

examples.en: How about meeting at the MTR station?
How about we reschedule to Sunday?

grammar.title: Time + place + verb
grammar.explain: The usual Cantonese order is who → when → where → what: 我哋 (ngo5 dei6) + 七點 (cat1 dim2) + 喺門口 (hai2 mun4 hau2) + 等 (dang2). The time word can also go first: 七點我哋喺門口等 (cat1 dim2 ngo5 dei6 hai2 mun4 hau2 dang2). But the place (喺 (hai2)…) always comes before the verb.

examples.en: We'll meet at seven at the entrance.
Tomorrow I'm having lunch with a friend in Central.

grammar.title: Verb + 唔到 (m4 dou2) = can't manage to
grammar.explain: 唔到 (m4 dou2) after a verb means you tried or wanted to but couldn't: 嚟唔到 (lai4 m4 dou2) 'can't make it', 搵唔到 (wan2 m4 dou2) 'can't find'.

examples.en: Sorry, I can't make it tonight.
I can't find you — where are you?

lines.en: Long time no see! How about hotpot this Friday?
Good idea! But I have to work on Friday night...
Then let's move it to Saturday night. Does eight o'clock work?
Works for me. Where shall we meet?
Outside Langham Place in Mong Kok. And don't be late again!
No problem, I'll definitely be on time!
(Saturday, 8:20) Hey, where are you? I've been waiting twenty minutes!
Sorry, sorry! I forgot to bring my Octopus card and had to go home to get it...
You said you'd definitely be on time!
I'm almost there, five more minutes! Dinner's on me tonight, OK?

questions.q: Why can't B do Friday?
Where and when do they agree to meet?
options: Langham Place in Mong Kok, Saturday at 8
Langham Place in Mong Kok, Friday at 8

questions.q: Why is B late?
options: B forgot the Octopus card and went home to get it

questions.q: How does B try to make up for being late?

units.title: Home & Gadgets
units.desc: Talk about your flat, switch things on and off, say what's lost or broken and get it fixed

words.note: Said fong2 on its own. Classifier 間 (gaan1): 一間房 (jat1 gaan1 fong2). Bedroom = 睡房 (seoi6 fong2).

ex.en: My room is very small.

words.note: Flats are described as 兩房一廳 (loeng5 fong2 jat1 teng1) 'two bedrooms, one living room'.

ex.en: The kids are watching TV in the living room.

words.note: Many people say ceoi4 fong2.

ex.en: Mum is cooking in the kitchen.

words.note: In HK flats the toilet and shower are usually in one room, all called 廁所 (ci3 so2).

ex.en: Excuse me, where's the toilet?
Can I open the window? It's so stuffy.
Remember to shut the door when you go out.

words.note: 開門 (hoi1 mun4) open the door, 開燈 (hoi1 dang1) turn on the light, 開冷氣 (hoi1 laang5 hei3) turn on the air-con.

ex.en: It's so hot, turn on the air-con!

words.en: to close / shut; to switch off
words.note: A very Cantonese character: a bar across a door. 閂燈 (saan1 dang1) = turn off the light.

ex.en: Turn off the light before you sleep.
It's too dark, please turn on the light.

words.note: 唔好 (m4 hou2) + verb = don't: 唔好開 (m4 hou2 hoi1) don't open it. Careful: 唔好食 (m4 hou2 sik6) can also be 唔 (m4) + 好食 (hou2 sik6) = not tasty; context tells you which.

ex.en: Don't turn off the light!

words.note: The machine is 冷氣機 (laang5 hei3 gei1), but people just say 部冷氣 (bou6 laang5 hei3).

ex.en: The air-con in the office is too strong.

words.note: Literally 'snow cupboard'.

ex.en: Is there any beer in the fridge?
The washing machine is so noisy.
My phone's battery is dead.

words.note: Everyday word. 充電 (cung1 din6) is the written/formal one.

ex.en: Can I charge my phone here?

words.note: 壞 (waai6) = bad/broken, 咗 (zo2) = it has happened.

ex.en: My computer is broken.

words.en: (end of sentence) that's how it is: explaining, 'you know'
words.fr: (fin de phrase) c'est comme ça, tu sais
words.note: 嘅 (ge3) + 啊 (aa3) merged. Adds a reason or insists on a fact: 好貴㗎 (hou2 gwai3 gaa3)! (it's expensive, you know!). In a question it shows surprise.

ex.en: This air-con was really expensive, you know!

words.note: 整返好 (zing2 faan1 hou2) = fix it back to working. Also 'make': 整嘢食 (zing2 je5 sik6) = make food.

ex.en: Do you know how to fix it?

words.en: repairman; (polite address to a tradesman or driver)
words.note: Call taxi drivers, chefs and repairmen 師傅 (si1 fu2).

ex.en: Sir, when can you come and fix it?

words.note: Classifier 條 (tiu4): 一條鎖匙 (jat1 tiu4 so2 si4).

ex.en: The key is by the door.

words.note: Literally 'not see anymore'. Two orders: 我唔見咗部手機 (ngo5 m4 gin3 zo2 bou6 sau2 gei1) I've lost my phone, or 部手機唔見咗 (bou6 sau2 gei1 m4 gin3 zo2) my phone's gone.

ex.en: I've lost my phone!

words.en: classifier: flat things (tables, beds, paper, tickets)

ex.en: Two tissues, please.

words.en: classifier: long thin things (keys, trousers, roads, fish)
words.fr: classificateur : objets longs et fins (clé, pantalon, rue, poisson)
words.note: 一條鎖匙 (jat1 tiu4 so2 si4) a key, 呢條褲 (ni1 tiu4 fu3) these trousers, 條路 (tiu4 lou6) the road.

ex.en: Whose key is this?
I want to buy a phone.
He bought a car.
That restaurant is really good.

sentences.en: My flat has two bedrooms and a living room.
The toilet is next to the kitchen.
The air-con is broken!
Remember to turn off the lights when you go out.
My phone is out of battery, I need to charge it.
Can you fix computers?
There are three phones in my home.
Don't open the window, it's raining.
The key is in the kitchen.
There's nothing in the fridge.
When will the repairman come?
Which room is yours?
I've lost my key, I can't get home!
Don't keep the air-con on all the time, it's expensive, you know.

grammar.title: Classifier + noun = 'the'
grammar.explain: Drop 呢 (ni1)/嗰 (go2): a classifier alone in front of a noun means 'the (one we both know)': 部冷氣 (bou6 laang5 hei3) = the air-con, 條鎖匙 (tiu4 so2 si4) = the key. English needs 'the' or 'my'; Cantonese just uses the classifier.

grammar.title: Choosing the classifier
grammar.explain: 部 (bou6) for machines, 張 (zoeng1) for flat things, 架 (gaa3) for vehicles, 間 (gaan1) for rooms and buildings, 條 (tiu4) for long thin things (keys, trousers, fish). If you're unsure, 個 (go3) is the safe default.

examples.en: I have a computer and a bike.
There are two beds in this room.

grammar.title: 開 (hoi1) and 閂 (saan1): open/close, on/off
grammar.explain: The same verbs work for doors, windows and devices: 開 (hoi1) = open / switch on, 閂 (saan1) = close / switch off.

grammar.title: 唔好 (m4 hou2) + verb = don't
grammar.explain: To tell someone not to do something, put 唔好 (m4 hou2) before the verb. Add 啊 (aa3) or 啦 (laa1) at the end to sound friendlier.

grammar.title: 㗎 (gaa3): 'it's like that, you know'
grammar.explain: Put 㗎 (gaa3) at the end to explain or insist on a fact, often giving a reason for what you just said. Compare 好貴 (hou2 gwai3) (it's expensive) with 好貴㗎 (hou2 gwai3 gaa3) (it's expensive, you know!).

examples.en: Don't open the window, it's noisy, you know.
That phone is really expensive, you know!

lines.en: Oh no, the air-con is broken!
What? It's thirty-four degrees today!
It's on, but it's not cold at all.
Have you tried turning it off and on again?
I tried, it still doesn't work.
Then call the repairman.
I did. The repairman isn't free until tomorrow.
What? So how are we going to sleep tonight?
Open the windows and turn on the fan!
No way, it's so noisy outside. I'm sleeping at my friend's place!

questions.q: What's wrong with the air-con?
How hot is it today?
When can the repairman come?
What does B decide to do, and why?
options: Sleep at a friend's place, because it's too noisy with the windows open
Sleep with the fan on, because it is quiet
Buy a new air-con, because it is cheap
Fix it himself, because the repairman is busy

units.title: Weather & Feelings
units.desc: Talk about the weather, typhoons and rain, pass on the forecast and say how you feel

ex.en: How's the weather today?
Hong Kong is so hot!

words.note: Muggy, stuffy heat = 翳焗 (ngai3 guk6), the classic HK summer feeling.
Used for weather, food and drinks: 凍檸茶 (dung3 ning2 caa4) = iced lemon tea. Pleasantly cool = 涼 (loeng4).

ex.en: Is it cold in Switzerland?

words.note: Literally 'rain falls'. 落緊雨 (lok6 gan2 jyu5) it's raining (right now), 落咗雨 (lok6 zo2 jyu5) it rained. Snow: 落雪 (lok6 syut3), which almost never happens in Hong Kong!

ex.en: It didn't rain today.

words.en: to be sunny (the sun comes out)

ex.en: The sun has come out!

words.note: 會 (wui5) + verb for what's going to happen: 會落雨 (wui5 lok6 jyu5) it's going to rain. Ask with 會唔會 (wui6 m4 wui5)？ Many speakers say 會 (wui6) with a low flat tone, especially at the start of 會唔會 (wui6 m4 wui5); both tones are understood.

ex.en: It's going to be very hot tomorrow.

words.note: 帶遮 (daai3 ze1) take an umbrella, 帶錢 (daai3 cin2) bring money. 唔記得帶 (m4 gei3 dak1 daai3) = forgot to bring.

ex.en: I forgot to bring my wallet.

words.note: Classifier 把 (baa2). 帶遮 (daai3 ze1) = take an umbrella.

ex.en: Remember to take an umbrella.

words.note: Literally 'wind strikes'. Typhoon signal = 風球 (fung1 kau4); No. 8 = 八號風球 (baat3 hou6 fung1 kau4), schools and offices close.

ex.en: There's a typhoon tomorrow, we don't have to go to work.

words.note: Signals 1, 3, 8, 9, 10. At No. 8 (八號風球 (baat3 hou6 fung1 kau4)) offices and schools close. 'Hoist' = 掛 (gwaa3).

ex.en: Will they hoist the No. 8 signal tonight?

words.note: The HK weather office that issues typhoon signals and rain warnings. Everyone checks its app.

ex.en: The Observatory says it's going to rain tomorrow.

words.note: Person + 話 (waa6) + what they said: 佢話唔嚟 (keoi5 waa6 m4 lai4) he says he's not coming. Not the same as 話 (waa2) in 電話 (din6 waa2) or 咩話 (me1 waa2).

ex.en: Mum says it's cold tonight.

words.en: (end of sentence) passing on what someone said; 'oh, I just noticed'
words.note: Use it for news you heard (天文台話會落雨喎 (tin1 man4 toi4 waa6 wui5 lok6 jyu5 wo3)) or something you just noticed: 落雨喎 (lok6 jyu5 wo3)! 'oh, it's raining!'

ex.en: Oh, it's raining!

words.note: 覺得 (gok3 dak1) + adjective = to feel …; also 'I think that …'.

ex.en: I feel a bit cold.

words.en: it seems; looks like; to be like
words.fr: on dirait ; avoir l'air ; ressembler à
words.note: At the start: 好似會落雨 (hou2 ci5 wui5 lok6 jyu5) it looks like rain. Also 'to look like': 好似 (hou2 ci5) + person, e.g. 好似你 (hou2 ci5 nei5) looks like you.

ex.en: You look really tired.

words.note: Before an adjective or verb: 真係好熱 (zan1 hai6 hou2 jit6) it's really hot. On its own as a question: 真係 (zan1 hai6)？ 'Really?'

ex.en: It's really hot today!

words.note: 唔開心 (m4 hoi1 sam1) = unhappy, upset.

ex.en: Why are you so happy today?

words.note: A very Cantonese character. 好攰 (hou2 gui6) = so tired.

ex.en: I worked ten hours today, I'm so tired.

words.note: Literally 'neck thirsty'.

ex.en: I'm so thirsty, I want some water.

words.note: Colloquial reading geng1. 唔使驚 (m4 sai2 geng1) = don't be afraid.

ex.en: My daughter is really scared of typhoons.

words.note: 嬲咗 (nau1 zo2) = has got angry. 唔好嬲 (m4 hou2 nau1) = don't be angry.

ex.en: Is your wife angry?

words.note: 好悶 (hou2 mun6) = so boring / I'm so bored.

ex.en: Staying home all the time is so boring.
I have an exam tomorrow, I'm so nervous.
Don't worry, I'm fine.

words.note: 唔舒服 (m4 syu1 fuk6) = unwell, not feeling good.

ex.en: I'm not feeling well, I want to go home.

sentences.en: It's very hot today, thirty-three degrees.
It's raining, did you bring an umbrella?
Is there going to be a typhoon tomorrow?
The Observatory has hoisted the No. 8 signal.
I think Hong Kong's winter isn't cold at all.
Are you tired? — Don't worry, I'm fine.
She's lost her phone, she's really upset.
Don't be angry, it's my fault.
It's really cold in Switzerland now, but in Hong Kong it's hot.
The sofa is really comfortable.
Luckily it didn't rain today.
Are you scared? — No, I'm not scared.
Looks like rain, take an umbrella.
The Observatory says it'll be cold tomorrow.

grammar.title: Adjectives are verbs: no 'to be'
grammar.explain: Never put 係 (hai6) before an adjective. Use 好 (hou2) (very / just linking) instead: 我好攰 (ngo5 hou2 gui6) = I'm tired. Without 好 (hou2) it sounds like a contrast.

grammar.title: 會 (wui5) = will / going to
grammar.explain: 會 (wui5) before a verb makes a prediction, especially about the weather. Negative: 唔會 (m4 wui5) won't. Question: 會唔會 (wui6 m4 wui5)…？

grammar.title: 話 (waa6) + 喎 (wo3): passing on news
grammar.explain: Person + 話 (waa6) + what they said reports speech. End with 喎 (wo3) to show it's news you're passing on: 'apparently'.

examples.en: The Observatory says there's going to be a typhoon.
Mum says she isn't coming tonight.

grammar.title: 有啲 (jau5 di1) = a bit, 一啲都唔 (jat1 di1 dou1 m4) = not at all
grammar.explain: 有啲 (jau5 di1) + adjective = 'a bit / rather', usually for something negative: 有啲凍 (jau5 di1 dung3), 有啲攰 (jau5 di1 gui6). 一啲都唔 (jat1 di1 dou1 m4) + adjective = 'not at all'.

examples.en: It's not hot at all today.

lines.en: Hey, the No. 8 signal is up! No work today!
Yay! I'm so happy!
But the wind is really strong outside. Are you scared?
A little. Have you closed the windows?
All closed. Is there any food in the fridge?
Only instant noodles… and two cans of beer.
Good enough! Let's watch TV at home.
Wait… the Observatory says it'll go down to No. 3 at two o'clock.
Oh no… so we still have to go to work in the afternoon?
Yep! I'm so annoyed!

questions.q: Why don't they have to go to work in the morning?
options: The No. 8 typhoon signal is up
Their office is closed for repairs

questions.q: What food do they have at home?
options: Instant noodles and two cans of beer

questions.q: What happens at two o'clock?
options: The signal goes down to No. 3
The signal goes up to No. 10

questions.q: How do they feel at the end?

units.title: Particles & Review
units.desc: Put it all together: review the little words that make Cantonese sound natural, plus everyday verbs for coming and going

words.note: In Cantonese 走 (zau2) means 'leave', not 'walk' (that's 行 (haang4)). 我走先喇 (ngo5 zau2 sin1 laa3) = I'm off (before you).

ex.en: I'm off, bye!

words.note: 唔知 (m4 zi1) = I don't know. 知唔知 (zi1 m4 zi1)…？ = do you know…? For knowing a person or a skill, use 識 (sik1).

ex.en: I don't know where he is.

words.en: to look for; to find; to get hold of
words.note: 搵到 (wan2 dou2) = found it, 搵唔到 (wan2 m4 dou2) = can't find it. 搵我 (wan2 ngo5) = get hold of me, call me.

ex.en: Who are you looking for?

words.note: 出去食飯 (ceot1 heoi3 sik6 faan6) = eat out. The opposite, coming in, is 入嚟 (jap6 lai4).

ex.en: Let's eat out tonight!

words.note: From the speaker's point of view: 返嚟 (faan1 lai4) come back here, 返去 (faan1 heoi3) go back there.

ex.en: What time are you coming back?

words.note: 快 (faai3) fast + 啲 (di1) a bit more. 快啲 (faai3 di1) 啦 (laa1)！ = come on, hurry! Slower = 慢啲 (maan6 di1).

ex.en: Hurry up, we're about to be late!

words.en: I'm fine; nothing's wrong; it's OK
words.note: Answer to 'are you OK?'. 你冇事吖嘛 (nei5 mou5 si6 aa1 maa3)？ = you're OK, right?

ex.en: I'm fine, don't worry.

words.note: Number + 次 (ci3): 一次 (jat1 ci3) once, 兩次 (loeng5 ci3) twice. 再講一次 (zoi3 gong2 jat1 ci3) = say it once more.

ex.en: I've been to Hong Kong three times.

words.en: downstairs; at the bottom of the building
words.note: Upstairs = 樓上 (lau4 soeng6). In HK 樓下 (lau4 haa6) often means the street right outside your building.

ex.en: I'll wait for you downstairs.

words.note: 附近有冇 (fu6 gan6 jau5 mou5)…？ = is there a … nearby? Here 近 (gan6) is read gan6, not kan5 as in 好近 (hou2 kan5).

ex.en: Is there an MTR station nearby?

words.note: Use 或者 (waak6 ze2) for "or" in statements and suggestions; in questions use 定係 (ding6 hai6). On its own, 或者 (waak6 ze2) also means "maybe".

ex.en: You can take the bus or the MTR.

sentences.en: I had dim sum yesterday, and I'm having it again today!
What are you watching? — I'm watching TV.
I've been to Hong Kong, but I haven't been to Macau yet.
Have you eaten? — Not yet.
It's stopped raining, let's go out!
Do you want this one or that one?
This one or that one, either is fine.
Is it still raining? — It's raining even harder!
You seem a bit tired.
I'm off, see you tomorrow!
As soon as I get home I'll take a shower.
These clothes are my sister's.
I don't know where he's gone.
Mum says to call her as soon as you're back.

grammar.title: Review: the end-of-sentence particles
grammar.explain: 啊 (aa3) softens a question · 呢 (ne1) 'and what about…?' · 啦 (laa1) suggests or urges · 喇 (laa3) something has changed · 㗎 (gaa3) explains a fact, 'you know' · 喎 (wo3) passes on news or something you just noticed. 啦 (laa1) and 喇 (laa3) differ only in tone!

examples.en: He says he isn't coming, apparently.

grammar.title: Review: 咗 (zo2), 緊 (gan2), 過 (gwo3), 未 (mei6)
grammar.explain: Right after the verb: 咗 (zo2) done · 緊 (gan2) in progress · 過 (gwo3) have ever done. Negatives: 冇 (mou5) + verb (didn't), 未 (mei6) + verb (not yet). Ask 'yet?' with verb + 咗 (zo2) + … + 未 (mei6)?

examples.en: I've eaten, but he's still eating.
I've had har gow, but I haven't tried siu mai yet.

grammar.title: Review: 都 (dou1), 又 (jau6), 再 (zoi3), 仲 (zung6), 先 (sin1), 就 (zau6)
grammar.explain: All go before the verb: 都 (dou1) also · 又 (jau6) again (it happened) · 再 (zoi3) again / then (next time) · 仲 (zung6) still · 先 (sin1) first (also at the very end) · 就 (zau6) then, right away.

examples.en: You eat first, I'll be right there.
You're late again! Don't be late again tomorrow.

grammar.title: Review: two kinds of 'or': 定係 (ding6 hai6) vs 或者 (waak6 ze2)
grammar.explain: 定係 (ding6 hai6) asks the listener to choose: 'A or B?' It only appears in questions, often shortened to 定 (ding6) in fast speech. 或者 (waak6 ze2) offers options in a statement: 'A or B, either is fine.'

examples.en: Are you going on Friday or Saturday?
I'll go on Friday or Saturday.
Hot or iced? — Either is fine.

lines.en: Have you had lunch yet?
Not yet, I'm still working.
It's already one-thirty! Eat first, come on!
OK. Do you want noodles or rice?
Either is fine. A cha chaan teng has opened downstairs, have you been?
