I went yesterday. It's cheap and really good!
Then let's go there again today!
Huh, looks like the boss is coming over…
Quick, let's go, right now!
Too late… he says he wants to come along too!

questions.q: Why hasn't B had lunch yet?
What time is it?
What does B say about the cha chaan teng downstairs?
What happens at the end?
options: The boss wants to join them for lunch
The boss asks B to keep working

units.title: Free Time & Sports
units.desc: Talk about your hobbies, how often you do things, and plan a weekend outing

ex.en: What are your hobbies?

words.fr: aller au cinéma / voir un film
words.note: 戲 (hei3) = film. Classifier is 套 tou3: 呢套戲 (ni1 tou3 hei3) 'this film'.

ex.en: Shall we go to the cinema tonight?

words.note: Literally 'walk mountain' — Hong Kong's favourite weekend sport.

ex.en: Hong Kong has lots of places to go hiking.
In summer I often go swimming at the beach.

words.note: 打 (daa2) for ball games played with the hands or a racket (on its own, 打波 (daa2 bo1) often means basketball); for a specific sport say 打籃球 (daa2 laam4 kau4) 'play basketball'.

ex.en: After school he plays ball with his classmates.

words.note: 踢 (tek3) = to kick.

ex.en: My little brother plays football every Sunday.

words.en: to sing; to go to karaoke
words.note: Going to karaoke is usually called 唱 (coeng3) + the English letter K, said 'coeng3 kei1'. 去唱歌 (heoi3 coeng3 go1) also often means going to karaoke.

ex.en: She sings really well.

words.note: 去旅行 (heoi3 leoi5 hang4) = go on a trip. Note hang4, not haang4 as in 行山 (haang4 saan1).

ex.en: Have you ever been to Japan on a trip?

words.note: One photo = 一張相 (jat1 zoeng1 soeng2). 'Take a photo of us' = 幫我哋影張相 (bong1 ngo5 dei6 jing2 zoeng1 soeng2).

ex.en: Could you take a photo of us, please?
I like listening to music when I take the MTR.

words.note: Goes AFTER the phrase: 我細個嘅時候 (ngo5 sai3 go3 ge3 si4 hau6) = when I was little.

ex.en: When I'm free I like listening to music.
My little brother plays video games all night.

words.note: Everyday word for reading. 讀書 duk6 syu1 means 'to study'.

ex.en: I usually read before going to sleep.

words.note: Literally 'cook things to eat'. 煮飯 (zyu2 faan6) also means 'to cook a meal'.

ex.en: At weekends I like cooking at home.

words.note: Also written 周末 (zau1 mut6).

ex.en: What do you usually do at the weekend?

words.en: often, all the time; all day
words.fr: souvent, tout le temps ; toute la journée
words.note: The most common spoken word for 'often'. Context tells you if it means 'all day'.

ex.en: She's always on her phone.

words.note: Same meaning as 成日 (seng4 jat6) but a bit more formal.

ex.en: We often go hiking together.
Sometimes I go to the cinema alone.

words.note: Less often than 有時 (jau5 si4). Usually followed by 都 (dou1) and 會 (wui5): 間中都會去 (gaan3 zung1 dou1 wui5 heoi3) 'I do go now and then'.

ex.en: I do play video games now and then.

words.note: 從來唔 (cung4 loi4 m4) + verb = never do. 從來冇 (cung4 loi4 mou5) + verb + 過 (gwo3) = have never (once) done.

ex.en: I never eat spicy food.

words.note: To exercise = 做運動 (zou6 wan6 dung6).

ex.en: Do you usually do any exercise?

words.note: 玩 (waan2) = to play, have fun — always a rising tone in everyday speech.

ex.en: Hiking is great fun!

words.note: Literally 'go to the street' — any going out of the house.

ex.en: It's raining, I don't want to go out.

words.note: Used for trips and outings: 幾點出發 (gei2 dim2 ceot1 faat3)? "What time do we leave?"

ex.en: Let's set off at eight tomorrow to go hiking.

sentences.en: At weekends I usually go hiking with friends.
What do you like doing in your free time?
I never play video games, but my little brother plays all the time.
It rained yesterday, so we didn't go hiking — we played games at home.
We occasionally go to karaoke after work.
Summer is too hot — I just want to go swimming at the beach.
Do you prefer playing football or basketball?
Sometimes I listen to music before going to sleep.
It's so beautiful here — take a photo of me!
He says he has no time to exercise, but he plays games all night.
Cooking is fun, but washing the dishes is boring.
I haven't read a book in ages.
This film is really good — have you seen it yet?
I've never been to Japan, but I really want to go.

grammar.title: How often: 成日 (seng4 jat6) · 有時 (jau5 si4) · 間中 (gaan3 zung1) · 從來唔 (cung4 loi4 m4)
grammar.explain: Frequency words go after the subject (and after any time word), right before the verb. 會 (wui5) 'would, tend to' often follows them.

examples.en: At weekends I often go swimming.

grammar.title: 去 (heoi3) + activity
grammar.explain: To 'go and do' something, put 去 (heoi3) straight before the activity — no extra word for 'to'. Ask with 去唔去 (heoi3 m4 heoi3).

grammar.title: …嘅時候 (ge3 si4 hau6) = when…
grammar.explain: Put 嘅時候 (ge3 si4 hau6) after a phrase to say 'when / while…'. It comes first, then the main sentence.

examples.en: When I'm free I like to cook.
When I was little I played football all the time.

dialogue.title: Hiking the Dragon's Back

lines.en: Hey, are you free this Saturday?
I'm free. What's the plan?
How about we go hiking on the Dragon's Back?
Sure! I've never been. Is it a hard walk?
Not hard, it's only about two hours of walking.
So what time do we set off?
Let's meet at Shau Kei Wan station at nine.
Nine?! So early! At weekends I usually don't get up till eleven!
If we go early the sun isn't as strong, and the photos are nicer too.
Fine, fine. I'll bring my camera!

questions.q: Where do they plan to go hiking?
How long is the walk, according to A?
What time does B usually get up at weekends?
Why does A want to start early?
options: The sun is less strong and photos are nicer
A has to work in the afternoon

gloss: to do, organise ("有咩搞" = what's the plan?)
(of the sun) to be strong; to bake in the sun

units.title: Health & Body
units.desc: Say what hurts, describe a cold or fever, and get through a visit to the doctor

words.note: 身體好 (san1 tai2 hou2) = in good health. 身體健康 (san1 tai2 gin6 hong1) is a common wish.

ex.en: My grandpa is in very good health.
My head feels a bit dizzy.

words.note: 肚餓 (tou5 ngo6) = hungry; 肚痛 (tou5 tung3) = stomach ache.

ex.en: I ate too much, my stomach is so full.
Wash your hands before eating.
I walked all day, my feet are killing me.

words.note: Many people say 'aan5' without ng-.

ex.en: I've been looking at the computer all day, my eyes are tired.
My throat is a bit sore.
Where does it hurt?

words.fr: mal de tête ; avoir mal à la tête

ex.en: I've had a headache since I got up this morning.
I ate seafood last night and now my stomach hurts.
Have you got a fever? Your head is very hot.
He's been coughing for a week.

words.en: cold / flu; to catch a cold
words.note: Also: 傷風 soeng1 fung1 (a common cold). Catching a chill = 凍親 (dung3 can1).

ex.en: I've caught a cold, I've got a runny nose.

words.note: Literally 'flow nose water'.

ex.en: The doctor says it's nothing serious.
If you're still coughing, go and see a doctor.
There's a clinic downstairs from my place.

words.note: 院 (jyun2) is jyun2 here (rising tone).

ex.en: My grandma is in hospital.
The doctor prescribed me two kinds of medicine.

words.note: In Cantonese you 'eat' medicine — even liquid medicine.

ex.en: Have you taken your medicine yet?

words.note: 係唔係好嚴重 (hai6 m4 hai6 hou2 jim4 zung6)? = Is it serious? 唔嚴重 (m4 jim4 zung6) = not serious.

ex.en: Don't worry, it's not serious.
You should rest for a couple of days.

words.note: 攞病假 lo2 beng6 gaa3 = take sick leave.

ex.en: I'm taking a day of sick leave today.

words.note: 返 (faan1) after an adjective = back to a normal state.

ex.en: Have you got better?
The floor is slippery, be careful!

sentences.en: I don't feel well today, I don't want to go to work.
You have a fever — go and see the doctor quickly.
My throat hurts and I keep coughing.
Take this medicine three times a day, after meals.
I've caught a cold, so I'm not going hiking tomorrow.
Drink more water and rest well.
Is the hospital far from here?
He fell playing football and hurt his foot.
Mind your hands, the stove is very hot!
Are you feeling better? — Much better, thanks.
I've got a bad headache today — maybe I'm too tired.
I rarely take medicine — I usually just sleep and get better.
Can I take a day of sick leave tomorrow?

grammar.title: Body part + 痛 (tung3)
grammar.explain: To say something hurts, put 痛 (tung3) after the body part. A classifier like 個 (go3) / 隻 (zek3) / 對 (deoi3) before the body part sounds very natural: 我個頭好痛 (ngo5 go3 tau4 hou2 tung3).

examples.en: My left foot hurts a bit.

grammar.title: 有啲 (jau5 di1) + adjective = a bit (unpleasant)
grammar.explain: 有啲 (jau5 di1) before an adjective means 'a bit / somewhat', usually for something negative. Compare 啲 (di1) after an adjective, which means '-er': 好啲 (hou2 di1) 'better'.

grammar.title: Verb + 返 (faan1) = back to normal
grammar.explain: 返 (faan1) after an adjective or verb means returning to the normal state: 好返 (hou2 faan1) 'get well again', 瞓返 (fan3 faan1) 'go back to sleep'.

examples.en: I woke up at three and couldn't get back to sleep.

dialogue.title: At the clinic

lines.en: Hello, where are you feeling unwell?
Doctor, my throat has been very sore since yesterday, and I keep coughing.
Do you have a fever?
A little. Last night it was thirty-eight degrees.
Open your mouth wide, let me have a look... It's a bit inflamed. You've caught a cold.
Is it serious? I have a football match on Saturday.
It's not serious. But you need to rest for two days — no football this week.
Oh... Then can you write me a sick note?
Sure. Take this medicine three times a day, after meals, and drink more water.
Thank you, doctor!

questions.q: What are B's symptoms?
options: Sore throat, cough and a slight fever
Sore eyes and a runny nose

questions.q: What does the doctor say B has?
Why is B worried?
options: B has a football match on Saturday
B is going on a trip

questions.q: How should B take the medicine?
options: Three times a day after meals

gloss: to start (尋日開始 = since yesterday)

units.title: Work & Study
units.desc: Talk about your job, colleagues, school and exams — and survive a job interview

words.note: 返公司 (faan1 gung1 si1) = go to the office.

ex.en: Which company do you work for?
I have lunch with my colleagues every day.

words.note: 份 (fan6) is the classifier for jobs. 工作 gung1 zok3 is the more formal word.

ex.en: Do you like your job?

words.note: 工作 (gung1 zok3) = work (formal); 經驗 (ging1 jim6) = experience. Day to day, people say 做嘢 (zou6 je5) or 返工 (faan1 gung1) for "work".

ex.en: Do you have any work experience?

words.note: In 開會 (hoi1 wui2) the 'meeting' syllable rises (wui2) — don't confuse it with 會 (wui5) 'will'.

ex.en: Sorry, I'm in a meeting, I'll call you back later.
I have to work overtime again tonight.

words.note: Send an email = 寄電郵 (gei3 din6 jau4) / 發電郵 (faat3 din6 jau4).

ex.en: Have you read the email I sent you?
She's been looking for a job for three months.
I have an interview tomorrow morning, I'm so nervous.

words.note: 加人工 (gaa1 jan4 gung1) = get a raise.

ex.en: The pay at this job isn't bad.
I'm so busy I want to quit!
Why are you studying Cantonese? — Because I like Hong Kong.

words.note: Cantonese often uses 因為 (jan1 wai6) … 所以 (so2 ji5) … together, unlike English.

ex.en: I'm busy today, so I can't go.

words.en: to be on holiday / day off

ex.en: When are you on holiday?
I've been really busy lately, no time to go hiking.

words.en: to study; to go to school
words.note: 你讀緊書 (nei5 duk6 gan2 syu1)？ = Are you still a student?

ex.en: Are you working or still studying?
I've been learning Cantonese for a year.
There are lots of students in the library.

words.note: Address a teacher as surname + 老師 (lou5 si1), e.g. 陳老師 (can4 lou5 si1).

ex.en: Our teacher speaks very fast.

words.note: Often said haau2 si5 (rising tone) in casual speech.

ex.en: I have an exam next week, I need to revise.

words.en: to revise, study for an exam

ex.en: Have you finished your homework?

words.note: Question: 明唔明白 (ming4 m4 ming4 baak6)? Short reply: 明白 (ming4 baak6) / 明 (ming4).

ex.en: Do you understand what I mean?
Sorry, I don't understand. Could you say it again?
Teacher, I have a question.

sentences.en: I'm so busy at work that I don't even have time for lunch.
The boss is in a meeting, come back in an hour.
Have you replied to that email yet?
I worked overtime until eleven last night, I'm exhausted.
My colleague is quitting, so the boss wants me to do her work too.
When I'm on holiday I don't want to read any work emails.
I don't understand this question, can you teach me?
The teacher gave us lots of homework again today.
Was the exam hard? — Not too hard, no problem.
She's studying in England, so her English is really good.
The pay is good, but I have to work overtime every day.
Since I came to London, I've been learning English.
Is your company big?

grammar.title: Verb + 到 (dou3) + result = so … that
grammar.explain: Put 到 (dou3) after an adjective or verb, then say the result: 忙到冇時間食飯 (mong4 dou3 mou5 si4 gaan3 sik6 faan6) 'so busy I have no time to eat'.

examples.en: I'm so tired I can't open my eyes.
He was so happy he jumped up.

grammar.title: Splitting verb + object: 辭咗職 (ci4 zo2 zik1), 讀過書 (duk6 gwo3 syu1)
grammar.explain: Many two-character verbs are really verb + object (辭職 (ci4 zik1), 讀書 (duk6 syu1), 開會 (hoi1 wui2), 搵工 (wan2 gung1)). Aspect markers and durations go in the middle: 開緊會 (hoi1 gan2 wui2), 辭咗職 (ci4 zo2 zik1), 搵咗三個月工 (wan2 zo2 saam1 go3 jyut6 gung1).

examples.en: I studied for four years at university.

grammar.title: 因為 (jan1 wai6)…所以 (so2 ji5)… = because … so …
grammar.explain: Unlike English, Cantonese happily uses both halves together. You can also drop either one.

examples.en: Because I have an exam, I'm not going out tonight.
Why did you quit? — Because the pay was too low.

lines.en: Please have a seat. Could you introduce yourself first?
Sure. I'm Wing, I studied design at university.
Do you have any work experience?
I worked at an advertising company for three years.
Then why do you want to change jobs?
Over there I had to work overtime till midnight every day — I want to learn new things.
Ha, we're not that busy here. Do you have any questions for us?
Um... may I ask, how much is the pay?
Let's talk about pay later. We'll let you know by email next week.
Great, thank you very much!

questions.q: What did Wing study at university?
How long did Wing work at the advertising company?
Why does Wing want to change jobs?
options: Too much overtime; wants to learn new things

questions.q: How will Wing hear back?

units.title: Opinions & Comparing
units.desc: Give your opinion, compare two things, agree and disagree — politely or not

words.note: More formal than 覺得 (gok3 dak1) — meetings, news, debates.

ex.en: I believe this plan isn't feasible.

words.fr: par rapport à (A 比 (bei2) B + adj)
words.note: A 比 (bei2) B 平 (peng4) = A is cheaper than B. Same sound as 畀 (bei2) 'give' — different character.

ex.en: Hong Kong is hotter than London.

words.note: The most colloquial comparison: 我高過你 (ngo5 gou1 gwo3 nei5) 'I'm taller than you'. Not the same as the aspect 過 (gwo3) 'have ever'.

ex.en: The MTR is faster than the bus.

words.note: 最 (zeoi3) + adjective/verb: 最平 (zeoi3 peng4) the cheapest, 最鍾意 (zeoi3 zung1 ji3) like best.

ex.en: Which restaurant do you like best?

words.note: Hongkongers queue for everything good — a long queue usually means the food is worth it.

ex.en: You always have to queue at this restaurant.
Eating at home is better than eating out.

words.note: A 冇 (mou5) B 咁 (gam3) + adj = A is not as … as B.

ex.en: Today isn't as hot as yesterday.

words.note: 快啲 (faai3 di1)! = hurry up! / faster! Opposite: 慢 (maan6) slow.

ex.en: You're speaking too fast — slower, please.
Getting around by MTR is really convenient.

words.note: 新開 (san1 hoi1) = newly opened (shop, restaurant). Opposite: 舊 (gau6) old.

ex.en: Is your phone new?
The two restaurants are about the same price.

words.note: A 同 (tung4) B 一樣 (jat1 joeng6) = A is the same as B.

ex.en: My phone is the same as yours.
What's the difference between these two?

words.note: Pairs with 但係 (daan6 hai6): 雖然 (seoi1 jin4)…但係 (daan6 hai6)… 'although…, (but)…'.

ex.en: Although it's expensive, it's really good.
Actually, I don't like spicy food much.
You should try their milk tea.
Maybe it'll rain this afternoon.
You'll definitely like it!
Expensive isn't necessarily good.
I don't agree with you.

words.note: 你講得啱 (nei5 gong2 dak1 ngaam1) = you're right. 啱啱 ngaam1 ngaam1 = just now.

ex.en: You're right, it's much cheaper here.

words.note: 唔錯 (m4 co3) = not bad (actually means 'good'). 冇錯 (mou5 co3) = exactly, that's right.

ex.en: Sorry, I took the wrong bus.

words.note: 抵食 (dai2 sik6) = good value food. Very HK!

ex.en: This set meal is only forty dollars, such good value!
What's your opinion?

sentences.en: I think Hong Kong summers are hotter than London's.
Taking the MTR is more convenient than taking a taxi, and cheaper too.
Which is the best cha chaan teng in Hong Kong?
Although Cantonese is hard, I think it's very interesting.
Because it's raining, I'm not going out today.
Actually the two phones are almost the same, only the colour is different.
This colour isn't as nice as that one.
You should go and see a doctor — you might have a fever.
He's definitely going to be late again.
Do you agree? — I agree, but my boss might not.
Sorry, I said it wrong — it's Thursday, not Tuesday.
Is hiking better, or swimming? — I prefer swimming.
My job is busier than before, but the pay is the same.

grammar.title: Comparing: A + adj + 過 (gwo3) + B
grammar.explain: The most natural spoken comparison: adjective then 過 (gwo3) then the thing compared. 比 (bei2) also works (A 比 (bei2) B + adj) but sounds a bit more formal. 'Much more' = add 好多 (hou2 do1) at the end.

examples.en: I'm taller than my big brother.
Hong Kong is much more expensive than London? Not necessarily!
This one is cheaper than that one.

grammar.title: A 冇 (mou5) B 咁 (gam3) + adj = not as … as
grammar.explain: To say A is less … than B, use 冇 (mou5) and 咁 (gam3).

examples.en: Swimming isn't as tiring as hiking.
My Cantonese isn't as good as yours.

grammar.title: Verb + 多啲 (do1 di1) = prefer
grammar.explain: 鍾意 (zung1 ji3) X 多啲 (do1 di1) means 'I like X more'. 多啲 (do1 di1) goes after the object, at the end.

examples.en: Do you prefer rice or noodles?

dialogue.title: Cha chaan teng vs. the new ramen place

lines.en: What shall we have for lunch? How about ramen? There's a new place.
Ramen again? I think the cha chaan teng downstairs is better than ramen.
The cha chaan teng is so noisy, and the waiters are so rude!
But it's cheap! Forty dollars gets you a meal and a milk tea — such good value.
The ramen place is a bit more expensive, but it's much nicer, and you can take photos too.
Are you going to eat or to take photos? The queue there is an hour long!
...You're right. We only have an hour for lunch.
So — cha chaan teng today, ramen on Saturday?
Deal! But on Saturday you're paying!

questions.q: Which restaurant does B prefer?
options: B wants to cook at home

questions.q: What does A dislike about the cha chaan teng?
options: It's noisy and the waiters are rude

questions.q: Why does A finally agree with B?
options: The ramen queue is an hour long and lunch is only an hour

questions.q: What is the final plan?
options: Cha chaan teng today, ramen on Saturday
Ramen today, cha chaan teng on Saturday

units.title: Festivals & Sayings
units.desc: Greet people at New Year and festivals, and use everyday set phrases with the right touch

words.note: THE Lunar New Year greeting. Kids jokingly add 利是逗來 (lai6 si6 dau6 loi4) 'now hand over the red packet!'

ex.en: Grandma, Happy New Year!

words.note: Works for both January 1st and Lunar New Year, but 恭喜發財 (gung1 hei2 faat3 coi4) is more typical for Lunar New Year.

ex.en: Happy New Year! All the best this year!

words.note: The go-to wish for elders; also at birthdays.

ex.en: Happy New Year, Grandma! Good health!

words.en: may everything go as you wish
words.fr: que tout aille selon vos souhaits
words.note: Pairs with almost any other greeting.

ex.en: Happy New Year, may everything go your way!

words.note: 祝 (zuk1) + person + wish: 祝你生日快樂 (zuk1 nei5 saang1 jat6 faai3 lok6) = happy birthday to you.

ex.en: Wishing Grandpa good health!

words.note: Said to children and students at New Year.

ex.en: Study hard this year — wishing you progress in your studies!

words.note: Married people give 利是 (lai6 si6) to children and unmarried adults at New Year, weddings and other happy occasions. Use new banknotes, and receive with both hands.

ex.en: Grandma gave me a red packet.

words.note: 收到 (sau1 dou2) = to have received: 收到你個訊息 (sau1 dou2 nei5 go3 seon3 sik1) = got your message.

ex.en: How many red packets did you get this year?

words.en: to go round collecting red packets
words.fr: faire la tournée des enveloppes rouges
words.note: What kids (and unmarried adults) do during New Year visits, saying greetings in exchange.

ex.en: The kids love collecting red packets the most at New Year.

words.fr: rendre visite pour le Nouvel An
words.note: Visiting relatives and friends in the first days of New Year, bringing fruit or sweets.

ex.en: On the first day of New Year we go to Grandma's to pay our respects.

words.note: Often shortened to 年卅晚 (nin4 saa1 aa6 maan5): 卅 (saa1 aa6) means 'thirty' and is said as two syllables. The family reunion dinner is that night.

ex.en: On New Year's Eve the flower market is packed.

words.fr: repas de réunion du Nouvel An
words.note: The whole family must be there; people travel far to attend.

ex.en: However busy you are, you have to come home for the reunion dinner.

words.note: Many foods are eaten for their 好意頭 (hou2 ji3 tau4), e.g. 年糕 (nin4 gou1) = 'higher every year', 髮菜蠔豉 (faat3 coi3 hou4 si2) sounds like 發財好市 (faat3 coi4 hou2 si5).

ex.en: At New Year you should eat things with a lucky meaning.

words.note: Used to scold or remind: don't argue, don't say unlucky things — it's New Year!

ex.en: It's New Year — don't argue!

words.note: Said right after someone mentions something unlucky (death, illness, failure), to cancel it out. Light-hearted but sincere.

ex.en: Heaven forbid! Don't talk such nonsense.

words.note: 我講笑咋 (ngo5 gong2 siu3 zaa3) = I'm only joking.

ex.en: Don't be cross, I was only joking.

words.note: 15th day of the 8th lunar month: family dinner, mooncakes, lanterns and moon-gazing.

ex.en: At Mid-Autumn the family has dinner together and admires the moon.

words.note: Classic filling: lotus-seed paste with salted egg yolk, 蓮蓉蛋黃 (lin4 jung4 daan2 wong2).

ex.en: This box of mooncakes was a gift from my colleague.

words.note: Done on the night of Mid-Autumn, often in parks or by the sea.

ex.en: We went to the beach to admire the moon.

words.note: 5th day of the 5th lunar month: dragon-boat races and sticky rice dumplings.

ex.en: Is the Dragon Boat Festival a public holiday?

words.note: Also written 粽 (zung2). Eaten at Dragon Boat Festival.

ex.en: My mum wraps rice dumplings herself every year.

words.note: For elders add 身體健康 (san1 tai2 gin6 hong1) or 長命百歲 (coeng4 meng6 baak3 seoi3).

ex.en: Happy birthday! Wishing you good health!

words.en: have a good trip (lit. 'tailwind all the way')
words.note: Some people avoid it for flights (planes take off into the wind) and say 一路平安 (jat1 lou6 ping4 on1) instead.

ex.en: Have a good trip, and let us know when you arrive!

words.note: Extremely common for festivals, sales, holidays.

ex.en: At New Year there are fireworks over the harbour, and it's packed.

words.note: Note the tones: maa1 maa1 fu1 fu1. In casual HK speech people more often say 麻麻地 (maa4 maa2 dei2) 'not that great' (a bit more negative) or 一般般 (jat1 bun1 bun1) 'average'.

ex.en: How's your Cantonese? — So-so.

words.en: go for it! you can do it!
words.note: Note the tone change: jau2 (not jau4). Cheering for exams, races, hard times.

ex.en: Exam tomorrow? Go for it!

sentences.en: When you see elders, remember to wish them a happy new year and good health.
At New Year, married people give red packets to unmarried people.
On New Year's Eve the whole family eats the reunion dinner together — very lively.
It's New Year — don't say unlucky things!
On Mid-Autumn night we go to the park to admire the moon and eat mooncakes.
At Dragon Boat Festival there are dragon boat races, and lots of people eat rice dumplings.
You're flying to the UK tomorrow? Have a safe trip!
The flower market on New Year's Eve is packed — such a crush!
Wow, long time no see! How have you been lately?
Have you eaten yet? If not, let's go for dim sum together.
My Cantonese is only so-so — I still need to keep learning.
Exam tomorrow? Go for it, we're all behind you!

grammar.title: Stacking four-character greetings
grammar.explain: Festival wishes are four-character set phrases. String two or three together, and pick one that fits the person: 身體健康 (san1 tai2 gin6 hong1) for elders, 學業進步 (hok6 jip6 zeon3 bou6) for students, 生意興隆 (saang1 ji3 hing1 lung4) for shop owners, 步步高升 (bou6 bou6 gou1 sing1) for someone with a career. 祝 (zuk1) + person + wish = 'I wish you…'.

examples.en: Happy New Year, and good health!
Wishing you progress in your studies and all the best!
Happy New Year, and may business boom!

grammar.title: Lucky and unlucky words (意頭 (ji3 tau4))
grammar.explain: Hongkongers care about how words sound. 4 sounds like 死 (sei2) (death), so some avoid the number; if someone says something unlucky, answer 大吉利是 (daai6 gat1 lai6 si6); if something breaks at New Year, rescue it with a lucky saying.

examples.en: Some people don't like the number 4, because 4 sounds like 'death'.
Heaven forbid! It's New Year, don't talk nonsense!

dialogue.title: New Year's Day at Grandma's

lines.en: Grandma, Happy New Year! Wishing you good health and all the best!
Good girl! Happy New Year! Here, a red packet for you.
Thank you, Grandma! But I'm thirty already — still getting red packets?
As long as you're not married, you still get one!
Ha ha, so if I never get married, I'll get red packets every year!
Heaven forbid! It's New Year — don't talk nonsense!
Only joking. I'm still full from yesterday's reunion dinner — what's good to eat today?
I made New Year cake — it brings good luck, you know.
Mmm, smells great! Where's my cousin? I haven't seen him for ages.
He's in the UK and couldn't come back this year; he phoned this morning to wish us a happy New Year.
Oh no! I've broken a bowl!
Never mind — 'it falls and blossoms, bringing wealth and glory'!
Tomorrow night there are fireworks over the harbour. Grandma, do you want to come and watch?
It'll be a sea of people — my old legs can't push through. You young ones go.
Then I'll take photos and bring them back to show you!

questions.q: Why does A still get a red packet at thirty?
Why does Grandma say 大吉利是 (daai6 gat1 lai6 si6)?
options: A joked about never getting married

questions.q: Why did Grandma make New Year cake?
options: Because there was no turnip cake
It was a gift from a neighbour

questions.q: What can we infer about the cousin?
options: He lives abroad and phoned instead of visiting
He went to see the fireworks

gloss: "it falls and blossoms" (said when something breaks at New Year)

units.title: Telling Stories
units.desc: Tell what happened: set the scene, move the story on, and deliver the twist

words.note: Used for general past habits: 我以前 (ngo5 ji5 cin4)… 'I used to…'.

ex.en: I used to work in Hong Kong.

words.note: Goes AFTER the event: 食飯之前 (sik6 faan6 zi1 cin4) = before eating. 三年之前 (saam1 nin4 zi1 cin4) = three years ago.

ex.en: Wash your hands before eating.

words.note: Very common in spoken storytelling, more colloquial than 然後 (jin4 hau6).

ex.en: I'll go to the bank first, then go grocery shopping.
In the end he still didn't come.

words.note: Carries relief: something you waited for finally happened.

ex.en: I've finally found a job!

words.note: Marks a discovery: 'oh, so that's how it is'.

ex.en: So you can speak Cantonese!
Suddenly the power went out — it was so dark!

words.note: 啱啱 (ngaam1 ngaam1) + verb = just did. Alone, 啱啱好 (ngaam1 ngaam1 hou2) = just right.

ex.en: He just left — you missed him by a step.

words.en: all along; the whole time; while
words.note: 一路 (jat1 lou6) A 一路 (jat1 lou6) B = doing A while doing B.

ex.en: He listens to music while he drives.

words.note: A bit more formal than 嗰陣 (go2 zan6).

ex.en: At the time I didn't know he was the boss.

words.note: Also 嗰陣時 (go2 zan6 si4). Put it after a clause: 我讀書嗰陣 (ngo5 duk6 syu1 go2 zan6) = when I was studying.

ex.en: When I was a student I loved playing ball.
What happened just now? Why are there so many police?

words.note: An event you went through, not work experience (that's 經驗 (ging1 jim6)).

ex.en: This is the most unforgettable experience of my life.
Grandma often tells me stories about the old days.

words.en: as a result; in the end
words.note: Introduces the (often bad) outcome.

ex.en: He didn't revise, so in the end he failed the exam.

words.en: had no choice but to; the only thing to do
words.note: 唯有 (wai4 jau5) + verb: the only option left. Very common when telling what went wrong.

ex.en: There were no taxis, so I had no choice but to walk.

words.note: Sets up a plan that then changed.

ex.en: I was originally going to go, but something came up.

words.note: Only for the past. For the future say 遲啲 (ci4 di1).

ex.en: Later on they got married.

words.note: The twist word: 'I expected X, but then…'.

ex.en: I thought it would be sunny, but then it rained.

words.note: 以為 (ji5 wai4) = what you thought, which turned out to be wrong. Compare 覺得 (gok3 dak1) = your opinion.

ex.en: I thought you'd gone home!

words.note: Shows surprise or disbelief.

ex.en: He actually forgot his own birthday!

words.note: Classic story opener.

ex.en: Once I fell asleep on the MTR and missed my stop.
When he got the news he rushed over immediately.

words.note: Verb + 冇耐 (mou5 noi2) = not long after…, e.g. 落車 (lok6 ce1) 冇耐 (mou5 noi2) = soon after getting off.

ex.en: Not long after I got home, it started raining.

words.note: 差啲 (caa1 di1) + bad thing = it almost happened (but didn't).

ex.en: I overslept this morning and was almost late.

sentences.en: I used to live in Kowloon; later I moved to Hong Kong Island.
Do you remember what happened when we first met?
I'd just left home when it suddenly started raining — and I had no umbrella!
We'd planned to go hiking, but a typhoon came, so we had to cancel.
I always thought he was a student — turns out he's the teacher!
I was so nervous at the time that I nearly failed the exam.
We waited half an hour and the bus finally came.
After hearing the news, he immediately phoned his family.
Back then I'd just graduated and didn't know a thing.
And then what happened? Hurry up and finish the story!
After that experience, I feel health matters more than money.
In the end we didn't go, and had hotpot at home instead.
When I was little I was scared of the dark — I had to sleep with the light on.
I actually bumped into my primary-school teacher in London!

grammar.title: 本來 (bun2 loi4)… 點知 (dim2 zi1)… — the plan and the twist
grammar.explain: 本來 (bun2 loi4) sets up what was supposed to happen; 點知 (dim2 zi1) ('who knew') brings in what actually happened. It's the backbone of most Cantonese anecdotes.

examples.en: I was going to go hiking, but then it rained.
I thought he wouldn't come — turns out he was first to arrive.

grammar.title: Clause + 嗰陣 (go2 zan6) = 'when …'
grammar.explain: To say 'when X happened', put the whole clause first and end it with 嗰陣 (go2 zan6) (or 嗰陣時 (go2 zan6 si4)). There's no word at the front like English 'when'.

examples.en: When I was little I lived in Canada.
When I got home, he was already asleep.

grammar.title: 一路 (jat1 lou6) A 一路 (jat1 lou6) B — doing two things at once
grammar.explain: Repeat 一路 (jat1 lou6) before each verb: 一路行一路食 (jat1 lou6 haang4 jat1 lou6 sik6) = eat while walking. On its own, 一路 (jat1 lou6) means 'all along' (我一路以為 (ngo5 jat1 lou6 ji5 wai4)…).

lines.en: Once, I took a minibus home from Mong Kok after work.
I was really tired then, and before long I fell asleep.
Suddenly the driver shouted that we had reached the last stop — I jumped up and got off.
Not long after getting off, I realised my wallet was gone!
Inside were my ID card and five hundred dollars in cash.
I went straight back to the terminus, but the minibus had already left.
At the time I really didn't know what to do, so I had no choice but to call the police.
I'd assumed I'd never get the wallet back.
But then the next day, a man phoned me.
It turned out he'd found my wallet on the minibus.
He found my business card inside, so he knew how to reach me.
He even came all the way from Tuen Mun to Mong Kok just to give it back to me.
I opened it and — amazingly — not a single dollar was missing!
I wanted to give him some money to say thanks, but he just smiled and said there was no need.
In the end I treated him to a milk tea, and we chatted while we drank.
That experience made me feel Hong Kong really is full of human warmth.

questions.q: Where did the narrator most likely lose the wallet?
How did the old man know whom to contact?
options: He found a business card in the wallet
He saw the narrator's name on the ID card
The police gave him the number

questions.q: What did the narrator expect after reporting the loss?
options: That the wallet would never come back
That the police would call the next day
That the driver would keep it
That only the cash would be missing

questions.q: Why does the story end with the narrator praising Hong Kong?
options: A stranger went out of his way and refused a reward
The police found the wallet quickly
The narrator found extra money in the wallet

units.title: Advanced Patterns
units.desc: Link ideas like a native: passives, 'even', 'as soon as', 'the more… the more', 'even if', 'rather'

words.note: 畀 (bei2) + doer + verb: 畀人偷咗 (bei2 jan4 tau1 zo2) = got stolen (by someone). Cantonese must name a doer; use 人 (jan4) if unknown.

ex.en: My bike got stolen.

words.note: Almost always passive: 畀人偷咗 (bei2 jan4 tau1 zo2) = got stolen.

ex.en: Someone stole my wallet!

words.note: 將 (zoeng1) + object + verb + where: moves the object before the verb. Slightly formal; very common in instructions.

ex.en: Please put the clothes in the washing machine.

words.note: Put the surprising item between 連 (lin4) and 都 (dou1).

ex.en: He's so busy he doesn't even have time to eat.

words.note: 一 (jat1) + first action, 就 (zau6) + second action.

ex.en: I go home as soon as I finish work.

words.note: 越嚟越 (jyut6 lai4 jyut6) + adjective or 鍾意 (zung1 ji3) etc.

ex.en: The weather is getting hotter and hotter.

words.note: 越 (jyut6) + verb, 越 (jyut6) + result.

ex.en: The more he talked, the angrier he got.

words.note: 諗住 (nam2 zyu6) + verb = to be thinking of doing. 諗下 (nam2 haa5) = think it over. Opinions use 覺得 (gok3 dak1).

ex.en: Let me think about it.

words.note: Often followed by 仲 (zung6) (also) or 都 (dou1) (all).

ex.en: Besides Cantonese, he can also speak French.

words.note: 就 (zau6) goes after the subject in the second clause.

ex.en: If it rains tomorrow, we won't go hiking.

words.note: A minimum condition that is enough.

ex.en: As long as it's fine tomorrow, we'll go hiking.

words.note: 唔肯 (m4 hang2) = refuses to: 佢唔肯食藥 (keoi5 m4 hang2 sik6 joek6) = he won't take his medicine.

ex.en: As long as you put in the practice, you'll definitely learn it.

words.note: 就算 (zau6 syun3) + condition, (subject) 都 (dou1) + result.

ex.en: Even if there's a typhoon tomorrow, I still have to work.

words.note: Usually with a question word: 無論幾貴 (mou4 leon6 gei2 gwai3) / 無論邊個 (mou4 leon6 bin1 go3).

ex.en: No matter how expensive, she wants to buy it.

words.note: 寧願 (ning4 jyun6) A，都唔 (dou1 m4) B = I'd rather A than B. Often said ning4 jyun2 in fast speech.

ex.en: I'd rather take the stairs than squeeze into the lift.

words.note: 搬屋 (bun1 uk1) = to move house. 搬嚟 (bun1 lai4) / 搬去 (bun1 heoi3) = move here / move there.

ex.en: I'm moving to London next year.
When you come to Hong Kong you must try egg tarts.

words.note: Adds impatience to a question.

ex.en: What on earth do you want?

words.note: Like 到底 (dou3 dai2), a bit more neutral.

ex.en: Who exactly ate all the cake?

words.note: Result is the opposite of what you'd expect.

ex.en: He didn't get angry — instead he burst out laughing.

words.note: Raises the stakes; a bit more formal than 連 (lin4)…都 (dou1).

ex.en: He loves Hong Kong so much he even taught himself Cantonese.
Hurry up, otherwise we won't make it.

words.note: A 先至 (sin1 zi3) B = only after A can B. Shorter: 先 (sin1).

ex.en: Only after finishing your homework can you play video games.
Getting to the airport from here takes at least an hour.

sentences.en: My phone got stolen — I can't even get back the photos on it.
As soon as he got my message he called me right away.
If you forgot your umbrella, just buy one at the convenience store.
Apart from Sunday, he has to work every day.
Do you actually know what you did wrong or not?
I'd rather cook myself than eat takeaway every day.
As long as it doesn't rain, we'll go for a beach barbecue tomorrow.
He likes Hong Kong more and more, and is even thinking of moving there.
Even if you failed the exam, there's no need to be so upset.
Please forward this email to the boss — he needs to read it as soon as he's back.
The older the kid gets, the more he looks like his dad.
You're all talk — when exactly are you going to actually do it?
No matter how busy he is, he calls home every week.

grammar.title: Passive with 畀 (bei2)
grammar.explain: Cantonese passive is 'thing + 畀 (bei2) + doer + verb (+咗 (zo2))'. Unlike English, the doer can't be dropped: if you don't know who, say 畀人 (bei2 jan4). It's mostly used for unpleasant events.

examples.en: I got told off by the boss.
His wallet was stolen by someone.
The cake got eaten by my little brother.

grammar.title: 就 (zau6) in the second half
grammar.explain: 一 (jat1)…就 (zau6) (as soon as), 如果 (jyu4 gwo2)…就 (zau6) (if), 只要 (zi2 jiu3)…就 (zau6) (as long as) all put 就 (zau6) right before the verb of the second clause — after its subject, never before it.

examples.en: As soon as I get home I take a shower.
As long as you're happy, that's fine.

grammar.title: 就算 (zau6 syun3) / 無論 (mou4 leon6) … 都 (dou1)
grammar.explain: Concessive clauses take 都 (dou1) in the second half: 'even if X, (subject) still Y'. 寧願 (ning4 jyun6) A 都唔 (dou1 m4) B works the same way: 'rather A than B'.

examples.en: Even if it rains, I'm still going.
No matter what you say, he won't listen.

dialogue.title: The noisy neighbours

lines.en: Why do you look so tired today?
I get woken up every morning by the renovation next door — not even Saturday is spared.
How long on earth are they still going to renovate?
They say at least two months. The more I think about it, the angrier I get.
Have you complained to the management office?
I have, but management says as long as they don't renovate at night, there's nothing they can do.
Then why don't you come and stay at my place for a while? There's a room nobody uses.
Thanks, but I'd rather put up with it for two months than trouble you.
Don't mention it! Even if you stayed half a year, it'd be no problem for me.
Really? Then besides paying my share, I can also cook and tidy up for you!
Great! If you're willing to cook, I should be the one thanking you.
It's a deal! I'll move my things over as soon as I finish work tonight.
Remember to bring a pillow — the room only has a bed.

questions.q: Why is B so tired?
options: The neighbours' renovation wakes B up every morning
B was out late on Saturday

questions.q: What did the management office say?
options: They can't stop it as long as the work isn't at night
The work will finish in two weeks
B should complain to the police
The renovation is not allowed on Saturdays

questions.q: Why did B first turn down A's offer?
options: B didn't want to trouble A

questions.q: What can we infer about the spare room?
options: It has a bed and nothing else

gloss: to be woken up by noise

units.title: HK Slang & Colloquial
units.desc: Sound like a local with everyday (clean) slang — and know when it fits

words.note: Casual but fine at work. 搞唔掂 (gaau2 m4 dim6) = can't handle it.

ex.en: Don't worry, I'll sort this out for you.

words.note: 放心啦 (fong3 sam1 laa1)! = relax, leave it to me. 唔放心 (m4 fong3 sam1) = to be uneasy.

ex.en: Don't worry, I'll sort this out for you.

words.note: 掂唔掂啊 (dim6 m4 dim6 aa3)? = Is it going OK? Casual.

ex.en: How's your new job going — all good?

words.note: Slang reading zeng3 (the standard reading zing3 means 'upright'). Casual, very common for food.

ex.en: The milk tea here is fantastic!

words.note: A warm compliment, often for kids or juniors.

ex.en: His son is really smart — he knows to help out.

words.note: As an adverb: 求其揀 (kau4 kei4 gaan2) = just pick any. As criticism: 做嘢好求其 (zou6 je5 hou2 kau4 kei4) = careless.

ex.en: Just pick any one, we're in a hurry.

words.note: Stands before the verb: 實得 (sat6 dak1) = it'll work for sure; 實冇問題 (sat6 mou5 man6 tai4) = no problem at all.

ex.en: If you don't bring an umbrella, you'll definitely regret it!

words.en: can't stand it; can't take it
words.note: Venting, informal. 頂得順 (ding2 dak1 seon6) = can bear it.

ex.en: My colleague talks on the phone all day long — I really can't stand it.

words.en: knock off (work); call it a day
words.note: More casual than 放工 (fong3 gung1); also said when finishing any task.

ex.en: What time do you knock off?

words.note: 今次 (gam1 ci3) = this time; 下次 (haa6 ci3) = next time. 次次 (ci3 ci3) = every time.

ex.en: Last time you chose — this time it's my turn!

words.en: get shot down; hit a wall
words.note: Literally 'bump into a board'. When a request is flatly refused.

ex.en: I asked the boss for leave and got shot down.

words.note: Literally 'the chicken ran off'.

ex.en: Buy one get one free today — don't miss out!

words.note: Opposite of 求其 (kau4 kei4). 講笑定認真 (gong2 siu3 ding6 jing6 zan1)? = joking or serious?

ex.en: She works very conscientiously — she's never sloppy.

words.note: Mostly describes the situation: 真係激氣 (zan1 hai6 gik1 hei3)! = how infuriating! 我好激氣 (ngo5 hou2 gik1 hei3) = I'm so fed up.

ex.en: I've waited half an hour and the bus still hasn't come — so annoying!

words.note: Mild, teasing; fine with friends but rude to strangers or elders.

ex.en: Are you nuts? Going hiking in this heavy rain!

words.note: Literally 'big wok'. 大鑊喇 (daai6 wok6 laa3)! = We're in trouble!

ex.en: Uh-oh! I forgot to bring my passport!

words.en: to chat idly; shoot the breeze
words.note: Also 'to talk big'. 吹下水 (ceoi1 haa5 seoi2) = have a chat.

ex.en: We chatted all evening.

words.note: Easy-going reply when given a choice. Can sound careless in formal settings.

ex.en: I'm easy, whatever you want to eat is fine.

words.note: Said of someone who agreed to come and then didn't.

ex.en: He always says he'll come, and always bails.

words.en: fall for a trap; get ripped off
words.note: For tourist traps, bad buys, overhyped restaurants.

ex.en: That restaurant was expensive and awful — we got had.

words.note: Handling a surprise on the spot. Positive: 識執生 (sik1 zap1 saang1) = resourceful.

ex.en: He wasn't prepared but spoke really well — he knows how to wing it.

words.note: Outraged disbelief. Strong but not vulgar.

ex.en: Are you kidding me? An hour's wait and still no table!

sentences.en: Everything's sorted — I can finally call it a day!
The set meal at this cha chaan teng is under fifty dollars — and it tastes great.
The new colleague is sharp — you only have to show him once.
Don't be so sloppy, otherwise you'll have to clean up the mess again.
Wow, you've had a haircut? Looks great!
It's unbearably hot today, I really don't want to go out.
Luckily I brought an umbrella, otherwise I'd be soaked.
He's made plans with me three times and bailed all three — so infuriating!
The tickets sold out in half an hour — I missed out again.
I was only joking, but he took it seriously.
Are you kidding? A bowl of noodles for a hundred dollars!
After work we went to a cha chaan teng for a chat.
You're OK, right? You look really pale.

grammar.title: Can / can't: verb + 得 (dak1) / 唔 (m4) + result
grammar.explain: Many slang verbs have a result part. Put 得 (dak1) in the middle for 'can', 唔 (m4) for 'can't': 搞得掂 (gaau2 dak1 dim6) / 搞唔掂 (gaau2 m4 dim6), 頂得順 (ding2 dak1 seon6) / 頂唔順 (ding2 m4 seon6). Questions repeat the verb: 頂唔頂得順 (ding2 m4 ding2 dak1 seon6)?

examples.en: I can't handle this on my own.
Don't worry, I can handle it.

grammar.title: Flavour particles: 喎 (wo3), 咋 (zaa3), 吖嘛 (aa1 maa3)
grammar.explain: Slang lives in the particles. 喎 wo3 = 'hey, I notice…' or passing on what someone said. 咋 zaa3 = 'only, that's all'. 吖嘛 aa1 maa3 = 'right? / you know' (checking or stating the obvious).

dialogue.title: Friday, knocking off

lines.en: Hey, finished for the day yet? I just got my report done.
Wow, that fast? I've still got an email to answer — I can't take it any more!
Don't answer it sloppily — last time you sent it to the wrong client and nearly landed in big trouble.
I know, I'm being really careful this time. Right — done!
Yay! Shall we go for dinner and have a chat?
Sure. Ah Ming says he's coming too — he won't bail again this time, I guess.
You're joking! Last time he said he'd come, and in the end he didn't show.
Where shall we eat? I'm easy, your call.
There's a dai pai dong in Wan Chai — cheap and fantastic, great value.
Last time I went to a place recommended online, and got totally ripped off.
Relax, I've been eating at this one for years — no traps.
Lucky I've got you! Then I'll call Ah Ming too.
Tell him if he bails again this time, I'll really be cross!
OK, OK! See you in a bit!

questions.q: What had A just finished when the conversation starts?
options: A phone call with Ah Ming

questions.q: Why does A warn B not to be sloppy with the email?
options: B once sent one to the wrong client
The boss is checking B's emails
The client is angry with A

questions.q: What can we infer about Ah Ming?
options: He has a habit of not showing up
He recommended the dai pai dong

questions.q: Why is B happy to let A choose the restaurant?
options: A knows the place well and B got burned last time
B has never eaten in Wan Chai
B doesn't like dai pai dongs

gloss: to send to the wrong person

units.title: News & Society
units.desc: Talk about everyday news: rents and salaries, traffic, weather warnings and the environment

words.note: To watch/read the news = 睇 (tai2) 新聞 (san1 man4). In everyday speech 新聞 (san1 man4) is very often said san1 man2, with a rising tone.

ex.en: I usually read the news on my phone on the MTR.

words.note: Hongkongers check it for rain and typhoon warnings.

ex.en: The weather forecast says there'll be showers tomorrow afternoon.
The government has launched a new recycling scheme.

words.note: Also 'economical'.

ex.en: The economy isn't good lately — lots of restaurants have no customers.
Population ageing is a big problem for society.

words.note: 啲後生 (di1 hau6 saang1) = young people. 你好後生 (nei5 hou2 hau6 saang1)! = you look so young!

ex.en: Young people these days love taking photos.

words.note: The usual word in news reports for 'ordinary people'.

ex.en: Many members of the public think rents are too high.
Hong Kong's public transport is very convenient.

words.note: 塞到死 (sak1 dou3 sei2) = jammed solid. A tailback is 車龍 (ce1 lung4), literally 'car dragon'.

ex.en: There's been a traffic accident, and now the traffic is terrible.
Property prices are so high, lots of young people can't afford a flat.

words.note: 升咗 (sing1 zo2) = has gone up. The opposite is 跌 (dit3), to fall.

ex.en: Property prices have gone up again this year.

words.note: 交租 (gaau1 zou1) = pay rent; 加租 (gaa1 zou1) = raise the rent.

ex.en: Rent takes up almost half of my salary.

words.note: The biggest hurdle to 買樓 (maai5 lau2).

ex.en: We've been saving for five years and still don't have enough for a down payment.

words.note: 儲錢 (cou5 cin2) = to save money; in this word many people say cou5 rather than cyu5. 儲咗 (cyu5 zo2) + time + 錢 (cin2) = have been saving for…

ex.en: I save a bit of money every month.
After my dad retires, he wants to move back to his hometown.
Hong Kong people are under a lot of pressure at work.
We should all do our bit to protect the environment.
Air pollution has been very bad lately.

words.note: 污染 (wu1 jim5) = pollution; 空氣 (hung1 hei3) = air.
Short for 環境保護 (waan4 ging2 bou2 wu6). 好環保 (hou2 waan4 bou2) = very green.

ex.en: Take your own water bottle when you go out — it's very eco-friendly.
Remember to recycle plastic bottles!
Typhoon signal number 8 is up, which affects many flights.
The number of tourists has increased a lot this year.
We should cut down on plastic bags.
This problem can't be solved in just a day or two.
According to the latest report, rents went up again last month.

words.note: Also tiu4 caa4.

ex.en: A survey says young people are sleeping less and less.

sentences.en: Did you see today's news? Rents have gone up again.
The Observatory says a typhoon is coming this weekend — better not go out to sea.
At rush hour the traffic is always jammed — the bus barely moved in half an hour.
Salaries have barely gone up, but everything keeps getting more expensive.
Many young people still live with their families, because rents are too high.
If property prices keep rising, how long will it take to save up a down payment?
The government wants to reduce waste, so it's encouraging people to recycle more.
The latest report says the number of people taking the MTR has gone up.
A lot of people are worried they won't have enough money after they retire.
Air pollution affects your health, especially for old people and children.
Is it true that if the black rainstorm signal is up, you don't need to go to work?
With so much work pressure, you should find time to relax.
Parking costs keep going up, so I'd rather take public transport.

grammar.title: Numbers in the news: 成 (sing4) and 百分之 (baak3 fan6 zi1)
grammar.explain: Percentages are 百分之 (baak3 fan6 zi1) + number (百分之五 (baak3 fan6 zi1 ng5) = 5%). In speech, tenths are often 成 (sing4): 一成 (jat1 sing4) = 10%, 兩成 (loeng5 sing4) = 20%, 三成半 (saam1 sing4 bun3) = 35%.

examples.en: Rent takes up 40% of his salary.

grammar.title: Reporting what you heard: 話 (waa6) / 聽講 (teng1 gong2) / 根據 (gan1 geoi3)
grammar.explain: To pass on news: X 話 (waa6)… (X says…), 聽講 (teng1 gong2)… (I heard that…), 根據 (gan1 geoi3)… (according to…, more formal). Add 喎 wo3 at the end to signal 'that's what they say'.

examples.en: The Observatory says it'll be 34 degrees tomorrow.
I heard the MTR is raising fares again next month.
According to the survey, most people think rents are too high.

lines.en: Have you seen today's news? It says rents rose again last month.
No wonder my landlord just told me he's raising the rent by two thousand dollars next month.
Two thousand? That's a lot! Your salary hasn't gone up that much.
Exactly. Rent already takes up almost half my salary — the pressure's huge.
Have you thought about moving to the New Territories? Rents there are a bit cheaper.
I have, but transport's a problem — getting to work would take at least an hour.
And at rush hour, if there's a jam, you could be late all the time.
Right. And transport costs money too — it might not actually be much cheaper.
There's also a survey in the news saying many young people want to move out, but don't have enough money.
With property prices this high, the down payment alone takes years of saving — how could they move out?
Has the government said how it'll solve it?
The report says they'll build more public housing, but you'll have to wait at least three or four years.
So what will you do? Renew the lease or move?
I'll stay put for now and save up more — I'll think about it later.
